data.retained_case_account: Court reporting describes an OpenAI emergency disclosure that reached the Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office through the FBI after Darren Zhou wrote threats against his ex-girlfriend in ChatGPT. Deputies compared those messages with anonymous threats that she had preserved. The sheriff’s booking entry lists May 29, 2026 as his arrest date. BocaNewsNow reports that he pleaded guilty on August 13 to written threats, aggravated stalking, and unlawful use of a two-way communication device. Adjudication was withheld, with eight years of probation, two years of GPS monitoring, and restrictions on contact and weapons. The accessible reporting cites court documents but does not reproduce the complete affidavit or plea order. It supports a police intervention and court restrictions, rather than proof that an attack would otherwise have occurred.

fields.account: Court reporting describes an OpenAI emergency disclosure that reached the Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office through the FBI after Darren Zhou wrote threats against his ex-girlfriend in ChatGPT. Deputies compared those messages with anonymous threats that she had preserved. The sheriff’s booking entry lists May 29, 2026 as his arrest date. BocaNewsNow reports that he pleaded guilty on August 13 to written threats, aggravated stalking, and unlawful use of a two-way communication device. Adjudication was withheld, with eight years of probation, two years of GPS monitoring, and restrictions on contact and weapons. The accessible reporting cites court documents but does not reproduce the complete affidavit or plea order. It supports a police intervention and court restrictions, rather than proof that an attack would otherwise have occurred.

record.title: Frankfurt police found a missing 16-year-old who had left a farewell letter on Taunusstraße within a day of her disappearance, after a judge-confirmed emergency order let the Bahnhofsviertel camera system's AI search for her face
record.summary: Frankfurt police found a missing 16-year-old in crisis within a day via a court-backed AI face search of Bahnhofsviertel cameras.
record.account: On 8 October 2025 a 16-year-old was reported missing after failing to return to the psychiatric facility in Hesse where she lived. A farewell letter pointed to an acute psychological crisis. Indications placed her in Frankfurt's Bahnhofsviertel. Citing imminent danger, Frankfurt's police president issued an emergency order, confirmed by a judge. So her photograph could be entered into the AI-assisted camera system running in the district since July 2025. It operates under the Hessian police law amended in February 2025. Late on 9 October the system flagged a match on Taunusstraße. A video operator checked it and a patrol confirmed it. Officers took the girl into protective custody and returned her to the child and adolescent psychiatric facility.
record.purpose: The Bahnhofsviertel Videoschutzanlage's AI performs real-time biometric remote identification. The Hessian police law amended in February 2025 allows this for narrow purposes such as finding missing persons. Locating a missing minor was that intended use. The Frankfurt police recorded the first confirmed success of a system in use since July 2025. The operational gain is modest.

later.note: By April 2026 the Hessian Greens had asked the Staatsgerichtshof to review the police-law amendment behind real-time face recognition, and Doña Carmen's Juanita Henning with the GFF had sued at the Frankfurt administrative court asking for referral to the Federal Constitutional Court; the system kept running, with an evaluation phase due from July 2026.
later.quote: Die lassen mit einem Normenkontrollantrag beim Staatsgerichtshof klären , ob die der Echtzeit-Fernidentifizierung zugrunde liegende Polizeigesetzänderung rechtens war. Eine Überprüfung der Rechtsgrundlage streben auch Juanita Henning und die GFF an. Sie haben beim Verwaltungsgericht Frankfurt beantragt, dass es die Abschnitte aus dem Polizeigesetz, die die Fernidentifizierung erlauben, dem Bundesverfassungsgericht vorlegt.

data.retained_case_account: On 8 October 2025 a 16-year-old was reported missing after failing to return to the psychiatric facility in Hesse where she lived. A farewell letter pointed to an acute psychological crisis. Indications placed her in Frankfurt's Bahnhofsviertel. Citing imminent danger, Frankfurt's police president issued an emergency order, confirmed by a judge. So her photograph could be entered into the AI-assisted camera system running in the district since July 2025. It operates under the Hessian police law amended in February 2025. Late on 9 October the system flagged a match on Taunusstraße. A video operator checked it and a patrol confirmed it. Officers took the girl into protective custody and returned her to the child and adolescent psychiatric facility.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: The police press release documents the system's contribution step by step. After a judge-confirmed emergency order, the girl's photo was entered into the database. Late on 9 October the AI produced an automated match alert for Taunusstraße. A video operator checked it and a patrol confirmed it in person. The police had only indications that she might be in the district, so the AI supplied the place and the moment. Human verification and the patrol did the rest. Whether and how soon conventional patrols would have found her is not reported.

fields.summary: Frankfurt police found a missing 16-year-old in crisis within a day via a court-backed AI face search of Bahnhofsviertel cameras.
fields.account: On 8 October 2025 a 16-year-old was reported missing after failing to return to the psychiatric facility in Hesse where she lived. A farewell letter pointed to an acute psychological crisis. Indications placed her in Frankfurt's Bahnhofsviertel. Citing imminent danger, Frankfurt's police president issued an emergency order, confirmed by a judge. So her photograph could be entered into the AI-assisted camera system running in the district since July 2025. It operates under the Hessian police law amended in February 2025. Late on 9 October the system flagged a match on Taunusstraße. A video operator checked it and a patrol confirmed it. Officers took the girl into protective custody and returned her to the child and adolescent psychiatric facility.

record.account: In 2023 a car driving north from Mexico approached the Point of Entry at San Ysidro. A U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) machine-learning model identified a suspicious pattern in its border-crossing history and flagged it for review. The review found 75 kilograms of narcotics hidden in the vehicle and led to the driver's arrest (DHS AI page, 27 November 2023). At the Axios AI+ Summit on 28 November 2023 Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas described a matching case. The Office of Field Operations model flagged a “truck” in 1.4 seconds that held about 75 kilograms of narcotics. DHS's 2024 AI Roadmap repeats it: a secondary-review flag yielding over 75 kg of drugs. No source names the drug or the seizure date.

data.retained_case_account: In 2023 a car driving north from Mexico approached the Point of Entry at San Ysidro. A U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) machine-learning model identified a suspicious pattern in its border-crossing history and flagged it for review. The review found 75 kilograms of narcotics hidden in the vehicle and led to the driver's arrest (DHS AI page, 27 November 2023). At the Axios AI+ Summit on 28 November 2023 Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas described a matching case. The Office of Field Operations model flagged a “truck” in 1.4 seconds that held about 75 kilograms of narcotics. DHS's 2024 AI Roadmap repeats it: a secondary-review flag yielding over 75 kg of drugs. No source names the drug or the seizure date.

record.title: Chile's “Fiscal Heredia” AI model may have identified a 10-member “encerrona” robbery gang; a court accredits 8 robberies
record.summary: In Operación Influencer (11 May 2023) prosecutors and PDI detained a gang of 10 aged 15–22 behind eight accredited violent robberies; the Fiscalía credits the university-built AI model Fiscal Heredia.
record.account: The Fiscalía de Chile's regional news release describes a joint investigation by Focos Occidente and the PDI's Brigada de Investigación Criminal. In the early hours of Thursday 11 May 2023 it led to 30 search warrants across Maipú, Pudahuel, Cerro Navia and other comunas. There were 17 detentions, ten linked to “encerronas” (robbery with intimidation or violence) whose perpetrators posted their robberies on TikTok. The release says they were identified through the software Fiscal Heredia (Herramienta para el Estudio del Delito Usando Inteligencia Artificial). It is an AI model developed by several universities and incorporated into the Ministerio Público in March 2023. It proposes probable participants from prosecution and police records for prosecutors and police to work up. The Noveno Juzgado de Garantía accredited the eight robberies. Four adults went to preventive detention and four adolescents remained in provisional internment. T13 quotes Fiscal Nacional Ángel Valencia saying the algorithm accelerates criminal analysis. It reports that after three members were arrested the AI searched their links to raise persons of interest later identified by victims. The OECD AI Incidents Monitor records the case.

data.retained_case_account: The Fiscalía de Chile's regional news release describes a joint investigation by Focos Occidente and the PDI's Brigada de Investigación Criminal. In the early hours of Thursday 11 May 2023 it led to 30 search warrants across Maipú, Pudahuel, Cerro Navia and other comunas. There were 17 detentions, ten linked to “encerronas” (robbery with intimidation or violence) whose perpetrators posted their robberies on TikTok. The release says they were identified through the software Fiscal Heredia (Herramienta para el Estudio del Delito Usando Inteligencia Artificial). It is an AI model developed by several universities and incorporated into the Ministerio Público in March 2023. It proposes probable participants from prosecution and police records for prosecutors and police to work up. The Noveno Juzgado de Garantía accredited the eight robberies. Four adults went to preventive detention and four adolescents remained in provisional internment. T13 quotes Fiscal Nacional Ángel Valencia saying the algorithm accelerates criminal analysis. It reports that after three members were arrested the AI searched their links to raise persons of interest later identified by victims. The OECD AI Incidents Monitor records the case.

record.title: INEC's Automated Biometric Identification System invalidates 2,780,756 ineligible voter registrations (22.6%) before Nigeria's 2023 election
record.summary: INEC chairman Mahmood Yakubu reported on 26 Oct 2022 that ABIS cleaning of 2021–22 registrations identified 2,780,756 (22.6%) double, underage or fake entries, leaving 9,518,188 valid new registrants.
record.account: The date is that of Professor Mahmood Yakubu's address to political parties in Abuja, reproduced by the Nigerian Democratic Report. He said the Continuous Voter Registration data (28 June 2021 to 31 July 2022) was cleaned with the Automated Biometric Identification System (ABIS). This identified 2,780,756 registrations (22.6%) as ineligible and invalidated them. Among them were double or multiple registrants, underage persons and fake registrations failing INEC's business rules. That left 9,518,188 valid post-ABIS registrations; 23 registration officers were identified for sanctions. On 12 September 2022, INEC commissioner Festus Okoye said 1,126,359 of 2,523,458 registrants (28 June 2021 to 14 January 2022) were found invalid and delisted. ABIS processing of later registrations was ongoing (Punch). BusinessDay later argued that some fake and underage registrants evaded ABIS and that invalidation rates were regionally lopsided. The vendor of ABIS is not named in the sources.

data.retained_case_account: The date is that of Professor Mahmood Yakubu's address to political parties in Abuja, reproduced by the Nigerian Democratic Report. He said the Continuous Voter Registration data (28 June 2021 to 31 July 2022) was cleaned with the Automated Biometric Identification System (ABIS). This identified 2,780,756 registrations (22.6%) as ineligible and invalidated them. Among them were double or multiple registrants, underage persons and fake registrations failing INEC's business rules. That left 9,518,188 valid post-ABIS registrations; 23 registration officers were identified for sanctions. On 12 September 2022, INEC commissioner Festus Okoye said 1,126,359 of 2,523,458 registrants (28 June 2021 to 14 January 2022) were found invalid and delisted. ABIS processing of later registrations was ongoing (Punch). BusinessDay later argued that some fake and underage registrants evaded ABIS and that invalidation rates were regionally lopsided. The vendor of ABIS is not named in the sources.

record.title: Telangana Police “Darpan” face-matching reunites Som Soni with his family after five years
record.summary: Darpan matched Som Soni, missing from Allahabad since 14 July 2015, to a boy in a Goalpara, Assam child home; reunited October 2020.
record.account: Darpan, a facial-recognition tool built by Telangana State Police, matches photographs of missing children against photographs of children lodged in child homes across the country. A routine matching run matched Som Soni to a boy police had found on 23 July 2015. He had been admitted to a child welfare center at Goalpara, Assam (spelled “Golapara” in the reports). Soni had gone missing from his home in Allahabad (Uttar Pradesh) on 14 July 2015 aged eight. ETV Bharat describes him as a resident of Handia in Allahabad. The case lay with Handia police station. Telangana Police notified Handia police. His parents traveled to Goalpara and identified him. The case was announced on 9 October 2020 by Swati Lakra, ADGP of the Telangana Police Women Safety Wing. The exact day of the reunion is not given.

data.retained_case_account: Darpan, a facial-recognition tool built by Telangana State Police, matches photographs of missing children against photographs of children lodged in child homes across the country. A routine matching run matched Som Soni to a boy police had found on 23 July 2015. He had been admitted to a child welfare center at Goalpara, Assam (spelled “Golapara” in the reports). Soni had gone missing from his home in Allahabad (Uttar Pradesh) on 14 July 2015 aged eight. ETV Bharat describes him as a resident of Handia in Allahabad. The case lay with Handia police station. Telangana Police notified Handia police. His parents traveled to Goalpara and identified him. The case was announced on 9 October 2020 by Swati Lakra, ADGP of the Telangana Police Women Safety Wing. The exact day of the reunion is not given.

details.value: PAWS was built to predict where poaching will occur and to prescribe patrol routes that maximize detection and removal of snares. The snare removals are exactly this intended benefit.

The paper itself cautions that the first QENP test's increased findings “may be partially explained by factors beyond the predictive model”. record.title: PAWS patrol-planning field test removes over 1,000 snares in Srepok Wildlife Sanctuary, Cambodia
record.summary: PAWS-directed ranger patrols in Srepok Wildlife Sanctuary removed over 1,000 snares in December 2018, versus 200–300 in a typical month.
record.account: PAWS (Protection Assistant for Wildlife Security) is a machine-learning pipeline that predicts poaching risk and plans patrols. It was field-tested with WWF Cambodia and Ministry of Environment rangers in Srepok Wildlife Sanctuary, Cambodia, from December 2018. Only the month is given, so the first day is used. Rangers received center coordinates of fifteen 3 x 3 km blocks chosen from PAWS risk predictions, without being told each block's risk class. In the first month, 72 rangers in teams of eight detected poaching in 32 cells and removed over one thousand snares. They had reported removing two or three hundred in an average month. Low-risk blocks yielded no poaching. A second trial ran February to March 2019.
record.purpose: PAWS was built to predict where poaching will occur and to prescribe patrol routes that maximize detection and removal of snares. The snare removals are exactly this intended benefit.
record.system: PAWS (Protection Assistant for Wildlife Security), enhanced iWare-E predictive model with Gaussian-process uncertainty and game-theoretic patrol planning
record.model_version: iWare-E with Gaussian-process weak learners trained on January 2015 to April 2018 dry-season data (Xu et al., ICDE 2020)
record.developer: Harvard University and University of Southern California (Milind Tambe and colleagues), with WWF, WCS and Uganda Wildlife Authority co-authors
record.deployer: WWF Cambodia with Cambodia Ministry of Environment rangers, Srepok Wildlife Sanctuary

ratings.reason: The ranger force's monthly snare removals rose from a reported two or three hundred to over one thousand. A material gain in patrol effectiveness for the operating team. A chi-squared test confirmed predictions discriminated risk (p = 0.023).

Over one thousand snares were removed from a sanctuary identified as a tiger-reintroduction site. The paper states each snare “represents the life of one animal potentially saved”. A material landscape-scale conservation benefit rather than a documented population-level change.

data.retained_case_account: PAWS (Protection Assistant for Wildlife Security) is a machine-learning pipeline that predicts poaching risk and plans patrols. It was field-tested with WWF Cambodia and Ministry of Environment rangers in Srepok Wildlife Sanctuary, Cambodia, from December 2018. Only the month is given, so the first day is used. Rangers received center coordinates of fifteen 3 x 3 km blocks chosen from PAWS risk predictions, without being told each block's risk class. In the first month, 72 rangers in teams of eight detected poaching in 32 cells and removed over one thousand snares. They had reported removing two or three hundred in an average month. Low-risk blocks yielded no poaching. A second trial ran February to March 2019.

fields.account: PAWS (Protection Assistant for Wildlife Security) is a machine-learning pipeline that predicts poaching risk and plans patrols. It was field-tested with WWF Cambodia and Ministry of Environment rangers in Srepok Wildlife Sanctuary, Cambodia, from December 2018. Only the month is given, so the first day is used. Rangers received center coordinates of fifteen 3 x 3 km blocks chosen from PAWS risk predictions, without being told each block's risk class. In the first month, 72 rangers in teams of eight detected poaching in 32 cells and removed over one thousand snares. They had reported removing two or three hundred in an average month. Low-risk blocks yielded no poaching. A second trial ran February to March 2019.

record.title: Global Fishing Watch data lets Kiribati fine a vessel US$1 million for fishing in the Phoenix Islands Protected Area
record.summary: Kiribati used the Google-Oceana-SkyTruth platform to document Marshalls 203 fishing illegally in PIPA; a US$1 million fine plus a US$1 million goodwill grant followed (reported September 2016).
record.account: Global Fishing Watch, developed by Oceana, SkyTruth and Google, launched publicly at the Our Ocean conference on 15 September 2016. It processes AIS tracks of tens of thousands of vessels. In Oceana's description, it uses machine learning and cloud computing to identify when they are fishing. Before launch, the Washington Post reported, the government of Kiribati used it to document how a tuna-fishing vessel had operated illegally. That was inside the Phoenix Islands Protected Area, declared off-limits to commercial fishing in early 2015, resulting in a US$1 million fine. Oceana board member Ted Danson wrote in Grist that the vessel was the Marshall Islands-flagged Marshalls 203. The fine was against its owner, Central Pacific Fishing Company. A goodwill arrangement to pay a further US$1 million as a grant came with it. Oceana's Jacqueline Savitz wrote in BBC Future in 2018 that the technology helped Kiribati extract a US$2 million fine, about 1% of GDP. The cited sources do not date the fine.

data.retained_case_account: Global Fishing Watch, developed by Oceana, SkyTruth and Google, launched publicly at the Our Ocean conference on 15 September 2016. It processes AIS tracks of tens of thousands of vessels. In Oceana's description, it uses machine learning and cloud computing to identify when they are fishing. Before launch, the Washington Post reported, the government of Kiribati used it to document how a tuna-fishing vessel had operated illegally. That was inside the Phoenix Islands Protected Area, declared off-limits to commercial fishing in early 2015, resulting in a US$1 million fine. Oceana board member Ted Danson wrote in Grist that the vessel was the Marshall Islands-flagged Marshalls 203. The fine was against its owner, Central Pacific Fishing Company. A goodwill arrangement to pay a further US$1 million as a grant came with it. Oceana's Jacqueline Savitz wrote in BBC Future in 2018 that the technology helped Kiribati extract a US$2 million fine, about 1% of GDP. The cited sources do not date the fine.

fields.account: Global Fishing Watch, developed by Oceana, SkyTruth and Google, launched publicly at the Our Ocean conference on 15 September 2016. It processes AIS tracks of tens of thousands of vessels. In Oceana's description, it uses machine learning and cloud computing to identify when they are fishing. Before launch, the Washington Post reported, the government of Kiribati used it to document how a tuna-fishing vessel had operated illegally. That was inside the Phoenix Islands Protected Area, declared off-limits to commercial fishing in early 2015, resulting in a US$1 million fine. Oceana board member Ted Danson wrote in Grist that the vessel was the Marshall Islands-flagged Marshalls 203. The fine was against its owner, Central Pacific Fishing Company. A goodwill arrangement to pay a further US$1 million as a grant came with it. Oceana's Jacqueline Savitz wrote in BBC Future in 2018 that the technology helped Kiribati extract a US$2 million fine, about 1% of GDP. The cited sources do not date the fine.

record.title: ActiveRemediation helps Flint locate hazardous water pipes
record.summary: ActiveRemediation helped Flint prioritize homes for inspection and replacement of lead or galvanized-steel service lines.
record.account: University researchers worked with Flint’s service-line replacement program from summer 2016. ActiveRemediation used property records and confirmed pipe materials to recommend inspections. Its held-out prediction accuracy was 91.6%. The researchers reported that the program had replaced hazardous lines at 4,419 homes by September 2017. A separate simulation estimated savings of about US$622 per replacement. Independent reporting later documented a decline in inspection success after the contractor changed its approach, alongside changes in geography and policy. A March 2019 court order required prioritization using the model’s address lists. The field evidence does not isolate the model’s effect on residents’ health or realized expenditure.

details.value: The provincial AI camera system was installed to monitor traffic routes and key areas and detect violations for investigation and enforcement, per Tuổi Trẻ. Identifying people gathering with weapons is that purpose.

details.label: AI contribution
details.value: The facial recognition of the provincial AI camera system supplied the identities. Tuổi Trẻ and VietNamNet say all 18 faces were accurately identified within about 30 minutes, after officers monitoring camera data had noticed the gathering. The summons, questioning and confessions were police work. The sources are three national outlets reporting the provincial police's own account, with no vendor, algorithm or accuracy figure given.

record.title: Phú Thọ provincial police AI cameras put faces to all 18 teenagers found gathering with weapons to fight in Việt Trì within about 30 minutes; all were summoned and confessed
record.summary: Tuổi Trẻ (14 June 2026): on the night of 13 June Phú Thọ police saw a group preparing weapons to fight in Việt Trì; the AI camera system identified all 18 faces in about 30 minutes; all confessed.
record.account: On the night of Saturday 13 June 2026, Phú Thọ provincial police detected a group of teenagers gathering in Việt Trì ward. Officers were monitoring and mining data from the camera system. The teenagers were preparing weapons and vehicles to fight and disturb public order, Tuổi Trẻ reported on 14 June. Within about 30 minutes the AI camera system of the provincial command center had accurately identified the faces of all 18 participants. They were aged 14 to 18. They came from Việt Trì, Vân Phú and Nông Trang wards and Phù Ninh and Bình Phú communes (Tuổi Trẻ, VietNamNet). Tiền Phong says the whole case was clarified in just over two hours. It says 17 of the 18 were pupils of schools including Vũ Thê Lang High School and Dữu Lâu Middle School. One had dropped out. data.retained_case_account: On the night of Saturday 13 June 2026, Phú Thọ provincial police detected a group of teenagers gathering in Việt Trì ward. Officers were monitoring and mining data from the camera system. The teenagers were preparing weapons and vehicles to fight and disturb public order, Tuổi Trẻ reported on 14 June. Within about 30 minutes the AI camera system of the provincial command center had accurately identified the faces of all 18 participants. They were aged 14 to 18. They came from Việt Trì, Vân Phú and Nông Trang wards and Phù Ninh and Bình Phú communes (Tuổi Trẻ, VietNamNet). Tiền Phong says the whole case was clarified in just over two hours. It says 17 of the 18 were pupils of schools including Vũ Thê Lang High School and Dữu Lâu Middle School. One had dropped out. It says the provincial police summoned all 18, and that at the police station they admitted the violations. No report says whether a fight took place.

fields.account: On the night of Saturday 13 June 2026, Phú Thọ provincial police detected a group of teenagers gathering in Việt Trì ward. Officers were monitoring and mining data from the camera system. The teenagers were preparing weapons and vehicles to fight and disturb public order, Tuổi Trẻ reported on 14 June. Within about 30 minutes the AI camera system of the provincial command center had accurately identified the faces of all 18 participants. They were aged 14 to 18. They came from Việt Trì, Vân Phú and Nông Trang wards and Phù Ninh and Bình Phú communes (Tuổi Trẻ, VietNamNet). Tiền Phong says the whole case was clarified in just over two hours. It says 17 of the 18 were pupils of schools including Vũ Thê Lang High School and Dữu Lâu Middle School. One had dropped out. It says the provincial police summoned all 18, and that at the police station they admitted the violations. No report says whether a fight took place.

fields.account: On the night of Saturday 13 June 2026, Phú Thọ provincial police detected a group of teenagers gathering in Việt Trì ward. Officers were monitoring and mining data from the camera system. The teenagers were preparing weapons and vehicles to fight and disturb public order, Tuổi Trẻ reported on 14 June. Within about 30 minutes the AI camera system of the provincial command center had accurately identified the faces of all 18 participants. They were aged 14 to 18. They came from Việt Trì, Vân Phú and Nông Trang wards and Phù Ninh and Bình Phú communes (Tuổi Trẻ, VietNamNet). Tiền Phong says the whole case was clarified in just over two hours. It says 17 of the 18 were pupils of schools including Vũ Thê Lang High School and Dữu Lâu Middle School. One had dropped out. It says the provincial police summoned all 18, and that at the police station they admitted the violations. No report says whether a fight took place.

Officers watching camera data at night who noticed the gathering
Reference images that let the system put names to 14-to-18-year-olds
Police able to summon the 18 and their families within hours
must_hold: Camera coverage of the gathering point with usable faces
The subjects are enrolled in the reference database
Police verification of each match before action

record.title: Origin Tech's AI satellite leak detection may have found over 800 leaks in an 18-week Thames Water trial, saving an estimated 8.7 million liters a day
record.summary: 18-week Origin Orbit trial on Thames Water's network: over 800 leaks found, est. 8.7 million liters a day saved (utility figures); 13-month contract followed, target 100 million liters a day.
record.account: Thames Water trialed Origin Orbit, the satellite leak-detection product of North East England start-up Origin Tech Ltd (founded 2019). The company and the utility describe it as using AI on satellite data to flag suspected underground leaks within a 30-meter search radius. Origin's co-founder John Marsden told the BBC the satellites pass over Swindon roughly every six days. He said they produce points on a map for Thames Water crews. Thames Water's statements say an 18-week trial found over 800 leaks across the network. They were reported by the BBC (20 May 2026) and reproduced in trade press. It saved an estimated 8.7 million liters of water a day, with several leaks running at more than 10 liters per second. On the strength of the trial, Thames Water signed a 13-month contract, launched in March 2026 per the utility's release. It deploys 20 specialist teams expected to find about 25 leaks a week each, and aims to cut leakage by 100 million liters a day. That makes it the first water company to integrate Origin Orbit into business-as-usual leakage operations. Origin Tech's own site adds a 2026 claim that Origin Orbit identified over 5,000 leaks (73.45 ML/d) across its customers. All figures originate with the utility and the vendor, and no regulator or independent measurement is among the sources. The trial dates are not given. Smart Water Magazine reported the result on 5 May 2026. Cambridgeshire County Council's AI inspection contract (April 2026) and Hertfordshire's ARRES robot (January 2024) have no outcomes on record. They are not among the sources.

fields.account: Thames Water trialed Origin Orbit, the satellite leak-detection product of North East England start-up Origin Tech Ltd (founded 2019). The company and the utility describe it as using AI on satellite data to flag suspected underground leaks within a 30-meter search radius. Origin's co-founder John Marsden told the BBC the satellites pass over Swindon roughly every six days. He said they produce points on a map for Thames Water crews. Thames Water's statements say an 18-week trial found over 800 leaks across the network. They were reported by the BBC (20 May 2026) and reproduced in trade press. It saved an estimated 8.7 million liters of water a day, with several leaks running at more than 10 liters per second. On the strength of the trial, Thames Water signed a 13-month contract, launched in March 2026 per the utility's release. It deploys 20 specialist teams expected to find about 25 leaks a week each, and aims to cut leakage by 100 million liters a day. That makes it the first water company to integrate Origin Orbit into business-as-usual leakage operations. Origin Tech's own site adds a 2026 claim that Origin Orbit identified over 5,000 leaks (73.45 ML/d) across its customers. All figures originate with the utility and the vendor, and no regulator or independent measurement is among the sources. The trial dates are not given. Smart Water Magazine reported the result on 5 May 2026. Cambridgeshire County Council's AI inspection contract (April 2026) and Hertfordshire's ARRES robot (January 2024) have no outcomes on record. They are not among the sources.

fields.summary: 18-week Origin Orbit trial on Thames Water's network: over 800 leaks found, est. 8.7 million liters a day saved (utility figures); 13-month contract followed, target 100 million liters a day.
fields.account: Thames Water trialed Origin Orbit, the satellite leak-detection product of North East England start-up Origin Tech Ltd (founded 2019). The company and the utility describe it as using AI on satellite data to flag suspected underground leaks within a 30-meter search radius. Origin's co-founder John Marsden told the BBC the satellites pass over Swindon roughly every six days. He said they produce points on a map for Thames Water crews. Thames Water's statements say an 18-week trial found over 800 leaks across the network. They were reported by the BBC (20 May 2026) and reproduced in trade press. It saved an estimated 8.7 million liters of water a day, with several leaks running at more than 10 liters per second. On the strength of the trial, Thames Water signed a 13-month contract, launched in March 2026 per the utility's release. It deploys 20 specialist teams expected to find about 25 leaks a week each, and aims to cut leakage by 100 million liters a day. That makes it the first water company to integrate Origin Orbit into business-as-usual leakage operations. Origin Tech's own site adds a 2026 claim that Origin Orbit identified over 5,000 leaks (73.45 ML/d) across its customers. All figures originate with the utility and the vendor, and no regulator or independent measurement is among the sources. The trial dates are not given. Smart Water Magazine reported the result on 5 May 2026. Cambridgeshire County Council's AI inspection contract (April 2026) and Hertfordshire's ARRES robot (January 2024) have no outcomes on record. They are not among the sources.

record.account: The Chemical Engineer reported on 5 May 2026, relaying UNEP's Methane Alert and Response System (MARS) figures. MARS had curbed 41 methane super-emitters since launching in 2023. Six significant sources had stopped emitting in 2026 following MARS alerts, including three in Turkmenistan and one each in Libya, Iraq and Kazakhstan. The largest source mitigated this year was a flare in Iraq, where operators diverted gas to a newer facility. The flare had released an estimated 1.7m tCO2e since 2023. The source appears to have been at a facility in the Zubair oil and gas field near Basra. The article reports that the operator Eni acknowledged running a leak detection and repair campaign at Zubair. Eni did not confirm closure of the specific source. The article says MARS uses data from 35 satellite instruments to identify large plumes and alert operators. UNEP's MARS page adds that IMEO couples satellite data with scientific expertise and advanced AI models. No date for the mitigation is given beyond 2026. UNEP's press releases were not available, and no UNEP case document for this source is on record.

data.retained_case_account: The Chemical Engineer reported on 5 May 2026, relaying UNEP's Methane Alert and Response System (MARS) figures. MARS had curbed 41 methane super-emitters since launching in 2023. Six significant sources had stopped emitting in 2026 following MARS alerts, including three in Turkmenistan and one each in Libya, Iraq and Kazakhstan. The largest source mitigated this year was a flare in Iraq, where operators diverted gas to a newer facility. The flare had released an estimated 1.7m tCO2e since 2023. The source appears to have been at a facility in the Zubair oil and gas field near Basra. The article reports that the operator Eni acknowledged running a leak detection and repair campaign at Zubair. Eni did not confirm closure of the specific source. The article says MARS uses data from 35 satellite instruments to identify large plumes and alert operators. UNEP's MARS page adds that IMEO couples satellite data with scientific expertise and advanced AI models. No date for the mitigation is given beyond 2026. UNEP's press releases were not available, and no UNEP case document for this source is on record.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: The trade press credits the mitigation to MARS alerts. Only UNEP's general page describes MARS as satellite-based with advanced AI models, so the AI contribution to this detection is not isolated. A single news item relaying the system operator documents the case. The named field operator declined to confirm closure of the specific source.

fields.summary: The Chemical Engineer (5 May 2026), relaying UNEP: the largest source mitigated in 2026 was an Iraqi flare, 1.7m tCO2e since 2023, apparently in the Zubair field; Eni did not confirm closure.
fields.account: The Chemical Engineer reported on 5 May 2026, relaying UNEP's Methane Alert and Response System (MARS) figures. MARS had curbed 41 methane super-emitters since launching in 2023. Six significant sources had stopped emitting in 2026 following MARS alerts, including three in Turkmenistan and one each in Libya, Iraq and Kazakhstan. The largest source mitigated this year was a flare in Iraq, where operators diverted gas to a newer facility. The flare had released an estimated 1.7m tCO2e since 2023. The source appears to have been at a facility in the Zubair oil and gas field near Basra. The article reports that the operator Eni acknowledged running a leak detection and repair campaign at Zubair. Eni did not confirm closure of the specific source. The article says MARS uses data from 35 satellite instruments to identify large plumes and alert operators. UNEP's MARS page adds that IMEO couples satellite data with scientific expertise and advanced AI models. No date for the mitigation is given beyond 2026. UNEP's press releases were not available, and no UNEP case document for this source is on record.

record.account: According to arrest papers cited by WCTV, Florida State University police responded to the St. Augustine parking garage at about 2:30 a.m. on Saturday 2 May 2026. ZeroEyes gun detection technology had detected an individual in black pointing a gun on the bottom level. Camera footage showed Tyler Farmer, 19, brandishing a loaded firearm at four other people. Officers found a Glock 19 handgun, stolen from Miller County, Georgia, in his waistband. He was charged with possessing a firearm on school property, unlawful carry, improper display of a firearm and grand theft of a firearm. He bonded out on Sunday. The Tallahassee Democrat, citing court records, says police responded to a “ZeroEyes camera notification” and that Farmer is not an FSU student. ZeroEyes layers over existing cameras and routes human-verified detections to police.

data.retained_case_account: According to arrest papers cited by WCTV, Florida State University police responded to the St. Augustine parking garage at about 2:30 a.m. on Saturday 2 May 2026. ZeroEyes gun detection technology had detected an individual in black pointing a gun on the bottom level. Camera footage showed Tyler Farmer, 19, brandishing a loaded firearm at four other people. Officers found a Glock 19 handgun, stolen from Miller County, Georgia, in his waistband. He was charged with possessing a firearm on school property, unlawful carry, improper display of a firearm and grand theft of a firearm. He bonded out on Sunday. The Tallahassee Democrat, citing court records, says police responded to a “ZeroEyes camera notification” and that Farmer is not an FSU student. ZeroEyes layers over existing cameras and routes human-verified detections to police.

Human analysts verify detections before alerts, so the AI's contribution is the initial detection. Both sources are local news citing arrest papers. Neither quantifies response time or states whether anyone else had called police.

fields.summary: At about 2:30 a.m. on 2 May 2026 ZeroEyes flagged a man pointing a gun in FSU's St. Augustine garage; officers found a stolen Glock 19 on Tyler Farmer and charged him, per court documents.
fields.account: According to arrest papers cited by WCTV, Florida State University police responded to the St. Augustine parking garage at about 2:30 a.m. on Saturday 2 May 2026. ZeroEyes gun detection technology had detected an individual in black pointing a gun on the bottom level. Camera footage showed Tyler Farmer, 19, brandishing a loaded firearm at four other people. Officers found a Glock 19 handgun, stolen from Miller County, Georgia, in his waistband. He was charged with possessing a firearm on school property, unlawful carry, improper display of a firearm and grand theft of a firearm. He bonded out on Sunday. The Tallahassee Democrat, citing court records, says police responded to a “ZeroEyes camera notification” and that Farmer is not an FSU student. ZeroEyes layers over existing cameras and routes human-verified detections to police.

record.title: Southern Water's sewer-monitor anomaly model flagged a forming fatberg in Rowner, Gosport, and a crew cleared it before any overflow into the River Alver
record.summary: Southern Water's AI sewer monitors flagged a forming fatberg in Rowner, Gosport; a crew cleared it before any overflow into the River Alver.
record.account: Southern Water runs around 34,000 sewer level monitors with machine learning. Its proactive operations control manager Daniel McElhinney says the system learns the normal behavior of sewers. He says it can tell a forming blockage from daily rushes or rain. Shortly before 22 April 2026 the sensors detected an abnormal flow in Rowner, Gosport, and alerted the control room. A crew jetted the sewer and found a fatberg of wet wipes and other unflushable items. The company said that, left unchecked, the sewer could have overflowed from a manhole into a surface water drain leading to the River Alver. The case was reported on 22 April 2026. A second flagged blockage at Warlands Lane, Shalfleet, Isle of Wight, was reported on 23 April.

fields.summary: Southern Water's AI sewer monitors flagged a forming fatberg in Rowner, Gosport; a crew cleared it before any overflow into the River Alver.
fields.account: Southern Water runs around 34,000 sewer level monitors with machine learning. Its proactive operations control manager Daniel McElhinney says the system learns the normal behavior of sewers. He says it can tell a forming blockage from daily rushes or rain. Shortly before 22 April 2026 the sensors detected an abnormal flow in Rowner, Gosport, and alerted the control room. A crew jetted the sewer and found a fatberg of wet wipes and other unflushable items. The company said that, left unchecked, the sewer could have overflowed from a manhole into a surface water drain leading to the River Alver. The case was reported on 22 April 2026. A second flagged blockage at Warlands Lane, Shalfleet, Isle of Wight, was reported on 23 April.

record.summary: New Civil Engineer (6 Jul 2026) quoting LNER's 9 Apr 2026 announcement: after a January 2026 Cambridgeshire defect caused over 10,000 delay minutes, One Big Circle's AIVR identified a developing fa...
record.account: New Civil Engineer's Tom Pashby reported on 6 Jul 2026. His story was about the system flagging a snake as a track defect on 3 July. LNER runs the Pantograph Damage Assessment System (PANDAS) and One Big Circle's Automated Intelligent Video Review (AIVR) on a number of its trains. They assess overhead line equipment and track and report potential damage to Network Rail. The article reproduces LNER's 9 April 2026 announcement. In January 2026 a train driver in Cambridgeshire reported a track defect. It caused over 10,000 delay minutes, multiple cancellations and a full day of disruption. A week later the AIVR system identified a minor fault near Retford with the potential to become a larger issue. Engineers carried out an overnight repair with no delay to passengers and zero delay minutes. An LNER spokesperson said the information is fed back to Network Rail to target areas for attention. A Network Rail spokesperson said the snake would be raised automatically as standard practice. Network Rail's own 2022 story describes AIVR as a phone-sized front-of-train device applying machine learning to video of more than 20,000 miles of track. The exact day of the Retford detection is not given. LNER's announcement itself and later Southeastern and South Western Railway AIVR releases are not among the sources.

data.retained_case_account: New Civil Engineer's Tom Pashby reported on 6 Jul 2026. His story was about the system flagging a snake as a track defect on 3 July. LNER runs the Pantograph Damage Assessment System (PANDAS) and One Big Circle's Automated Intelligent Video Review (AIVR) on a number of its trains. They assess overhead line equipment and track and report potential damage to Network Rail. The article reproduces LNER's 9 April 2026 announcement. In January 2026 a train driver in Cambridgeshire reported a track defect. It caused over 10,000 delay minutes, multiple cancellations and a full day of disruption. A week later the AIVR system identified a minor fault near Retford with the potential to become a larger issue. Engineers carried out an overnight repair with no delay to passengers and zero delay minutes. An LNER spokesperson said the information is fed back to Network Rail to target areas for attention. A Network Rail spokesperson said the snake would be raised automatically as standard practice. Network Rail's own 2022 story describes AIVR as a phone-sized front-of-train device applying machine learning to video of more than 20,000 miles of track. The exact day of the Retford detection is not given. LNER's announcement itself and later Southeastern and South Western Railway AIVR releases are not among the sources.

fields.account: New Civil Engineer's Tom Pashby reported on 6 Jul 2026. His story was about the system flagging a snake as a track defect on 3 July. LNER runs the Pantograph Damage Assessment System (PANDAS) and One Big Circle's Automated Intelligent Video Review (AIVR) on a number of its trains. They assess overhead line equipment and track and report potential damage to Network Rail. The article reproduces LNER's 9 April 2026 announcement. In January 2026 a train driver in Cambridgeshire reported a track defect. It caused over 10,000 delay minutes, multiple cancellations and a full day of disruption. A week later the AIVR system identified a minor fault near Retford with the potential to become a larger issue. Engineers carried out an overnight repair with no delay to passengers and zero delay minutes. An LNER spokesperson said the information is fed back to Network Rail to target areas for attention. A Network Rail spokesperson said the snake would be raised automatically as standard practice. Network Rail's own 2022 story describes AIVR as a phone-sized front-of-train device applying machine learning to video of more than 20,000 miles of track. The exact day of the Retford detection is not given. LNER's announcement itself and later Southeastern and South Western Railway AIVR releases are not among the sources.

record.title: After a UNEP MARS alert, operators repair a failed ball valve that released 175 t of methane in one week at the Aerial oil and gas field, Alberta, a week after detection (April 2026)
record.summary: Trade press relaying UNEP's August 2026 snapshot: a 175 t/week methane plume at Alberta's Aerial field in April 2026 was traced to a failed ball valve on pigging equipment and repaired within a week.
record.account: The Chemical Engineer reported on 4 September 2026 on UNEP's monthly snapshot of the biggest satellite-detected methane plumes recorded in August. UNEP confirmed that operators had plugged a source at the Aerial oil and gas field in southeastern Alberta, Canada. The source had released 175 t of methane (4,900 tCO2e) in a single week in April 2026. The cause was a failed ball valve connected to pigging equipment. Operators completed the repair one week after the plume was first detected. The repair followed an alert issued under UNEP's Methane Alert and Response System (MARS). The article states that UNEP does not name suspected or known operators. It states that since 2023 MARS has sent over 3,500 alerts but confirmed just 43 mitigation cases. UNEP's MARS page states that IMEO uses data from more than 30 satellite instruments. It couples that with scientific expertise and advanced AI models to notify governments and companies. The August 2026 UNEP snapshot itself is not among the sources; UNEP's snapshot page now carries the September 2026 update, which does not mention Canada. UNEP's press pages were not available and are not among the sources. The case rests on one trade-press report relaying UNEP.

data.retained_case_account: The Chemical Engineer reported on 4 September 2026 on UNEP's monthly snapshot of the biggest satellite-detected methane plumes recorded in August. UNEP confirmed that operators had plugged a source at the Aerial oil and gas field in southeastern Alberta, Canada. The source had released 175 t of methane (4,900 tCO2e) in a single week in April 2026. The cause was a failed ball valve connected to pigging equipment. Operators completed the repair one week after the plume was first detected. The repair followed an alert issued under UNEP's Methane Alert and Response System (MARS). The article states that UNEP does not name suspected or known operators. It states that since 2023 MARS has sent over 3,500 alerts but confirmed just 43 mitigation cases. UNEP's MARS page states that IMEO uses data from more than 30 satellite instruments. It couples that with scientific expertise and advanced AI models to notify governments and companies. The August 2026 UNEP snapshot itself is not among the sources; UNEP's snapshot page now carries the September 2026 update, which does not mention Canada. UNEP's press pages were not available and are not among the sources. The case rests on one trade-press report relaying UNEP.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: The report credits the repair to a MARS alert and UNEP's confirmation. Only UNEP's general page describes MARS detection and analysis as using satellites with advanced AI models. The AI contribution to this specific alert is not isolated. One news item relaying the system operator's snapshot documents the event, and the snapshot itself is not among the sources.

fields.summary: Trade press relaying UNEP's August 2026 snapshot: a 175 t/week methane plume at Alberta's Aerial field in April 2026 was traced to a failed ball valve on pigging equipment and repaired within a week.
fields.account: The Chemical Engineer reported on 4 September 2026 on UNEP's monthly snapshot of the biggest satellite-detected methane plumes recorded in August. UNEP confirmed that operators had plugged a source at the Aerial oil and gas field in southeastern Alberta, Canada. The source had released 175 t of methane (4,900 tCO2e) in a single week in April 2026. The cause was a failed ball valve connected to pigging equipment. Operators completed the repair one week after the plume was first detected. The repair followed an alert issued under UNEP's Methane Alert and Response System (MARS). The article states that UNEP does not name suspected or known operators. It states that since 2023 MARS has sent over 3,500 alerts but confirmed just 43 mitigation cases. UNEP's MARS page states that IMEO uses data from more than 30 satellite instruments. It couples that with scientific expertise and advanced AI models to notify governments and companies. The August 2026 UNEP snapshot itself is not among the sources; UNEP's snapshot page now carries the September 2026 update, which does not mention Canada. UNEP's press pages were not available and are not among the sources. The case rests on one trade-press report relaying UNEP.

record.title: AI smoke-detection camera installed for Arizona Public Service spots early signs of the March 2026 Diamond Fire in Coconino National Forest; crews hold it under 7 acres
record.summary: AP: an APS AI camera detected smoke on a March 2026 afternoon and crews contained the Diamond Fire before 7 acres; the Arizona Daily Sun's account of 26 March 2026 gives the timeline but no camera.
record.account: The Associated Press reported on 4 May 2026 that artificial intelligence detected something resembling smoke on a camera feed from Arizona's Coconino National Forest. The report is by Dorany Pineda and Brittany Peterson, on record in the KPBS and Courthouse News republications. The detection came on a March afternoon. One of dozens of AI cameras installed for the utility Arizona Public Service had spotted early signs. The fire came to be known as the Diamond Fire. Firefighters raced to the scene and contained it before it grew past 7 acres (2.8 hectares). AP says APS has nearly 40 active AI smoke-detection cameras and plans 71 by summer's end. APS meteorologist Cindy Kobold says the technology notifies the utility about 45 minutes faster on average than the first 911 call. Pano AI, launched in 2020 and charging around $50,000 a year per camera, counts APS among its customers. It says it detected 725 wildfires in the US last year. AP does not state outright which company made the camera that spotted the Diamond Fire. The Arizona Daily Sun (staff report, 26 March 2026) reports that a small fire later named the Diamond Fire began shortly after 2 p.m. on Thursday. It started just north of Lake Mary Road, about three miles south-east of Lake Mary Road and Beulah Boulevard. That is south of Pine Canyon Golf Club and east of Flagstaff Pulliam Airport. It reached seven acres by 3:16 p.m. according to WatchDuty. Its forward progress was stopped at 3:37 p.m., about 80 minutes after the first report, and it was 100% contained at 6:09 p.m. The Daily Sun does not mention a camera, the Coconino National Forest or who made the first report. The two accounts are matched by the fire's name, month and size. No official incident record naming the camera was found; InciWeb's “Diamond Fire” is a June 2023 Scottsdale fire. The Daily Sun reported the fire that Thursday.

data.retained_case_account: The Associated Press reported on 4 May 2026 that artificial intelligence detected something resembling smoke on a camera feed from Arizona's Coconino National Forest. The report is by Dorany Pineda and Brittany Peterson, on record in the KPBS and Courthouse News republications. The detection came on a March afternoon. One of dozens of AI cameras installed for the utility Arizona Public Service had spotted early signs. The fire came to be known as the Diamond Fire. Firefighters raced to the scene and contained it before it grew past 7 acres (2.8 hectares). AP says APS has nearly 40 active AI smoke-detection cameras and plans 71 by summer's end. APS meteorologist Cindy Kobold says the technology notifies the utility about 45 minutes faster on average than the first 911 call. Pano AI, launched in 2020 and charging around $50,000 a year per camera, counts APS among its customers. It says it detected 725 wildfires in the US last year. AP does not state outright which company made the camera that spotted the Diamond Fire. The Arizona Daily Sun (staff report, 26 March 2026) reports that a small fire later named the Diamond Fire began shortly after 2 p.m. on Thursday. It started just north of Lake Mary Road, about three miles south-east of Lake Mary Road and Beulah Boulevard. That is south of Pine Canyon Golf Club and east of Flagstaff Pulliam Airport. It reached seven acres by 3:16 p.m. according to WatchDuty. Its forward progress was stopped at 3:37 p.m., about 80 minutes after the first report, and it was 100% contained at 6:09 p.m. The Daily Sun does not mention a camera, the Coconino National Forest or who made the first report. The two accounts are matched by the fire's name, month and size. No official incident record naming the camera was found; InciWeb's “Diamond Fire” is a June 2023 Scottsdale fire. The Daily Sun reported the fire that Thursday.

fields.account: The Associated Press reported on 4 May 2026 that artificial intelligence detected something resembling smoke on a camera feed from Arizona's Coconino National Forest. The report is by Dorany Pineda and Brittany Peterson, on record in the KPBS and Courthouse News republications. The detection came on a March afternoon. One of dozens of AI cameras installed for the utility Arizona Public Service had spotted early signs. The fire came to be known as the Diamond Fire. Firefighters raced to the scene and contained it before it grew past 7 acres (2.8 hectares). AP says APS has nearly 40 active AI smoke-detection cameras and plans 71 by summer's end. APS meteorologist Cindy Kobold says the technology notifies the utility about 45 minutes faster on average than the first 911 call. Pano AI, launched in 2020 and charging around $50,000 a year per camera, counts APS among its customers. It says it detected 725 wildfires in the US last year. AP does not state outright which company made the camera that spotted the Diamond Fire. The Arizona Daily Sun (staff report, 26 March 2026) reports that a small fire later named the Diamond Fire began shortly after 2 p.m. on Thursday. It started just north of Lake Mary Road, about three miles south-east of Lake Mary Road and Beulah Boulevard. That is south of Pine Canyon Golf Club and east of Flagstaff Pulliam Airport. It reached seven acres by 3:16 p.m. according to WatchDuty. Its forward progress was stopped at 3:37 p.m., about 80 minutes after the first report, and it was 100% contained at 6:09 p.m. The Daily Sun does not mention a camera, the Coconino National Forest or who made the first report. The two accounts are matched by the fire's name, month and size. No official incident record naming the camera was found; InciWeb's “Diamond Fire” is a June 2023 Scottsdale fire. The Daily Sun reported the fire that Thursday.

details.label: Focus
details.value: Cybersecurity

details.label: Purpose
details.value: Claude Code is Anthropic's agentic coding tool, built to read a codebase, edit files, run commands and connect to external tools over MCP. Wiz used it, with IDA MCP, to automate reverse engineering of GitHub's compiled binaries. Analyzing code for flaws is within that general purpose. The benefit was an application of what the tool was built to do rather than a departure from it.

details.label: AI contribution
details.value: The AI's documented contribution is speed of analysis, on the researchers' own account. Wiz writes that AI-augmented reverse-engineering tooling, particularly IDA MCP, let it rapidly analyze GitHub's compiled binaries and reconstruct internal protocols. Wiz says that speed would not have been feasible manually. Sagi Tzadik told Dark Reading that with AI tools it took under 48 hours from idea to working exploit. The Register adds that the team used Claude Code “to take a lot of the legwork out of the process”. The hypothesis, the exploit, the report and the fix were human work. Six named Wiz researchers confirmed RCE on GHES 3.19.1 and wrote what GitHub called a thorough report. GitHub's security and engineering teams reproduced the bug within 40 minutes and deployed the fix. GitHub's own post, the CVE record and the GHES release notes describe a Bug Bounty report without mentioning AI. The AI-assistance claim therefore rests on Wiz and on outlets quoting Wiz. Wiz's write-up, in the text as read, names IDA MCP and not Claude.

record.title: Wiz Research's AI-augmented reverse engineering of GitHub's closed-source git binaries, with Claude Code and IDA MCP, finds a critical push-option injection giving remote code execution on GitHub.com and GitHub Enterprise Server; GitHub reproduces it in 40 minutes, patches github.com by 7:00 pm UTC on 4 March 2026 and finds no exploitation
record.summary: Wiz's AI-aided reverse engineering found a critical GitHub RCE (CVE-2026–3854); github.com was patched the same day, no exploitation found.
record.account: On 4 March 2026 Wiz Research reported a critical remote code execution (RCE) flaw to GitHub, later CVE-2026–3854. It sat in GitHub's internal git infrastructure. Git push options were not sanitized before being written into internal headers. Any authenticated user could therefore run arbitrary commands on GitHub's servers with a single git push. Wiz says AI-augmented tooling made the research feasible, particularly automated reverse engineering of GitHub's compiled binaries with IDA MCP. The Register reports that the team used Claude Code and went from idea to working exploit in under 48 hours. GitHub reproduced the bug within 40 minutes and deployed a fix to github.com at 7:00 pm UTC that day. It released GitHub Enterprise Server (GHES) patches from 10 March, and found no exploitation.
record.purpose: Claude Code is Anthropic's agentic coding tool, built to read a codebase, edit files, run commands and connect to external tools over MCP. Wiz used it, with IDA MCP, to automate reverse engineering of GitHub's compiled binaries. Analyzing code for flaws is within that general purpose. The benefit was an application of what the tool was built to do rather than a departure from it.

ratings.reason: GitHub closed a critical remote code execution hole in its git push pipeline within hours of the report. The fix reached github.com at 7:00 pm UTC on 4 March 2026. GitHub also shipped patches for six GitHub Enterprise Server release lines. Wiz earned what GitHub calls one of the highest rewards in the history of its Bug Bounty program. The loss avoided is hypothetical. GitHub's forensic investigation found that no other account had triggered the code path. No customer data was accessed, modified or exfiltrated. The benefit is an exposure closed rather than a demonstrated loss prevented.

ai_role.statement: The AI's documented contribution is speed of analysis, on the researchers' own account. Wiz writes that AI-augmented reverse-engineering tooling, particularly IDA MCP, let it rapidly analyze GitHub's compiled binaries and reconstruct internal protocols. Wiz says that speed would not have been feasible manually. Sagi Tzadik told Dark Reading that with AI tools it took under 48 hours from idea to working exploit. The Register adds that the team used Claude Code “to take a lot of the legwork out of the process”. The hypothesis, the exploit, the report and the fix were human work. Six named Wiz researchers confirmed RCE on GHES 3.19.1 and wrote what GitHub called a thorough report. GitHub's security and engineering teams reproduced the bug within 40 minutes and deployed the fix. GitHub's own post, the CVE record and the GHES release notes describe a Bug Bounty report without mentioning AI. The AI-assistance claim therefore rests on Wiz and on outlets quoting Wiz. Wiz's write-up, in the text as read, names IDA MCP and not Claude.

must_hold: AI output has to be confirmed by exploit, not trusted. Wiz confirmed RCE on a GHES 3.19.1 instance before reporting. That is why GitHub could validate the report in 40 minutes.

fields.account: On 4 March 2026 Wiz Research reported a critical remote code execution (RCE) flaw to GitHub, later CVE-2026–3854. It sat in GitHub's internal git infrastructure. Git push options were not sanitized before being written into internal headers. Any authenticated user could therefore run arbitrary commands on GitHub's servers with a single git push. Wiz says AI-augmented tooling made the research feasible, particularly automated reverse engineering of GitHub's compiled binaries with IDA MCP. The Register reports that the team used Claude Code and went from idea to working exploit in under 48 hours. GitHub reproduced the bug within 40 minutes and deployed a fix to github.com at 7:00 pm UTC that day. It released GitHub Enterprise Server (GHES) patches from 10 March, and found no exploitation.

revisions.change: Record drafted from the OECD Monitor entry and the cited sources. the date observed is 4 March 2026, the day Wiz reported the flaw and GitHub fixed github.com (GitHub's post: root cause identified at 5:45 pm UTC, fix deployed at 7:00 pm UTC; Wiz and The Verge say within six hours of the report; GitHub's standfirst says under two hours); the Monitor's 28 April 2026 is the public-disclosure date. Filed as benefit created or restored: the AI-assisted discovery produced a concrete fix for an identifiable organization, and the harm avoided is hypothetical because GitHub's forensic investigation found no exploitation. The AI tool is named differently by the sources: The Register (byline Connor Jones on the page as first read) and WebProNews say Claude Code, and WebProNews names Anthropic; Wiz's own write-up credits “AI-augmented tooling, particularly automated reverse engineering using IDA MCP”, and a search of its text as read found no occurrence of “Claude” or “Anthropic”, so the record names Claude Code on The Register's authority and IDA MCP on Wiz's. No Claude model is named anywhere. Severity: the CVE record (CNA GitHub) gives CVSS 4.0 8.7; The Register reports an 8.8 rating from NIST. GHES patch dates: Wiz's timeline says 10 March 2026, the 3.14.25 release notes are dated 12 March 2026. The Wiz post is marked as written by the makers because it is the discoverer's own account of its tooling, although Wiz is not the AI vendor; GitHub's post is the beneficiary's statement and is not flagged. Experienced vulnerability researchers: six named Wiz authors formed the hypothesis and built and confirmed a working exploit. They wrote what GitHub called a thorough report that clearly demonstrated the impact.

fields.account: On 4 March 2026 Wiz Research reported a critical remote code execution (RCE) flaw to GitHub, later CVE-2026–3854. It sat in GitHub's internal git infrastructure. Git push options were not sanitized before being written into internal headers. Any authenticated user could therefore run arbitrary commands on GitHub's servers with a single git push. Wiz says AI-augmented tooling made the research feasible, particularly automated reverse engineering of GitHub's compiled binaries with IDA MCP. The Register reports that the team used Claude Code and went from idea to working exploit in under 48 hours. GitHub reproduced the bug within 40 minutes and deployed a fix to github.com at 7:00 pm UTC that day. It released GitHub Enterprise Server (GHES) patches from 10 March, and found no exploitation.

record.title: Istanbul police's AVCI messaging-analysis system used for the first time in a 10 February 2026 drug operation across 14 provinces: 325 suspects detained and remanded, 69 dealer groups closed
record.summary: Istanbul police's AI-based AVCI system, first used 10 February 2026 in a 14-province drug operation: 325 detained and remanded, 69 groups closed.
record.account: AVCI (Açık Kaynak İstihbaratı Analiz Sistemi, Open Source Intelligence Analysis System) is an AI-supported program. The Istanbul Police Department's narcotics and cybercrime divisions built it in-house with a special software team. Police chief Selami Yıldız ordered the work. It infiltrates closed groups and channels on end-to-end encrypted messaging apps. It analyzes messages, voice notes, photos and location data. It decodes dealer slang, recovers deleted messages, links fake profiles and maps group hierarchies. Anadolu Agency reported on 6 April 2026 that AVCI was first used on 10 February 2026. The drug operation was centered on Istanbul and ran across 14 provinces. 325 suspects were detained. All 325 referred to court were remanded in custody. 69 messaging-app groups were closed.

data.retained_case_account: AVCI (Açık Kaynak İstihbaratı Analiz Sistemi, Open Source Intelligence Analysis System) is an AI-supported program. The Istanbul Police Department's narcotics and cybercrime divisions built it in-house with a special software team. Police chief Selami Yıldız ordered the work. It infiltrates closed groups and channels on end-to-end encrypted messaging apps. It analyzes messages, voice notes, photos and location data. It decodes dealer slang, recovers deleted messages, links fake profiles and maps group hierarchies. Anadolu Agency reported on 6 April 2026 that AVCI was first used on 10 February 2026. The drug operation was centered on Istanbul and ran across 14 provinces. 325 suspects were detained. All 325 referred to court were remanded in custody. 69 messaging-app groups were closed.

fields.account: AVCI (Açık Kaynak İstihbaratı Analiz Sistemi, Open Source Intelligence Analysis System) is an AI-supported program. The Istanbul Police Department's narcotics and cybercrime divisions built it in-house with a special software team. Police chief Selami Yıldız ordered the work. It infiltrates closed groups and channels on end-to-end encrypted messaging apps. It analyzes messages, voice notes, photos and location data. It decodes dealer slang, recovers deleted messages, links fake profiles and maps group hierarchies. Anadolu Agency reported on 6 April 2026 that AVCI was first used on 10 February 2026. The drug operation was centered on Istanbul and ran across 14 provinces. 325 suspects were detained. All 325 referred to court were remanded in custody. 69 messaging-app groups were closed.

record.account: The New Indian Express (6 January 2026) reported on a 77-year-old resident of Binnypet, Bengaluru. In November 2025 a man calling himself Yatin Shah contacted him. He claimed to be an adviser with IIFL Wealth Management and promised assured allotment of pre-IPO shares. The victim first transferred Rs 5 lakh for a supposed ICICI Prudential AMC pre-IPO and was shown profits in a digital wallet. Over the following weeks he made multiple RTGS transfers totaling Rs 67.10 lakh. When requests to withdraw even part of the funds were denied, he searched for details about the company and its representatives using ChatGPT. It reportedly flagged complaints, inconsistencies in company credentials and indicators associated with investment fraud. He then approached the police, who registered a case under the Information Technology Act. The police said that efforts were under way to trace the money. Deccan Herald (Prajwal D'Souza, 6 January 2026) framed the ChatGPT response as saving him from losing more money. No police official is named, no recovery is reported and the victim is unnamed.

fields.account: The New Indian Express (6 January 2026) reported on a 77-year-old resident of Binnypet, Bengaluru. In November 2025 a man calling himself Yatin Shah contacted him. He claimed to be an adviser with IIFL Wealth Management and promised assured allotment of pre-IPO shares. The victim first transferred Rs 5 lakh for a supposed ICICI Prudential AMC pre-IPO and was shown profits in a digital wallet. Over the following weeks he made multiple RTGS transfers totaling Rs 67.10 lakh. When requests to withdraw even part of the funds were denied, he searched for details about the company and its representatives using ChatGPT. It reportedly flagged complaints, inconsistencies in company credentials and indicators associated with investment fraud. He then approached the police, who registered a case under the Information Technology Act. The police said that efforts were under way to trace the money. Deccan Herald (Prajwal D'Souza, 6 January 2026) framed the ChatGPT response as saving him from losing more money. No police official is named, no recovery is reported and the victim is unnamed.

record.title: Ho Chi Minh City street AI cameras identify a masked burglar by gait, build, clothing and face; Tân Hưng ward police detain him within two days
record.summary: HCMC street AI cameras identified a masked burglar who took two laptops and 14 million VND on 23 December 2025; police held him on 24 Dec.
record.account: Early on 23 December 2025 an intruder entered a rented room at 62 Street 51, Tân Hưng ward, Ho Chi Minh City. He took two laptops and the wallet, identity papers and bank card of the tenant, H.A.T., 33. From his account, 14 million VND was withdrawn. He reported it that morning. Tân Hưng Ward Police and the Criminal Police Division used the street AI camera system. It analyzed the masked man's gait, build, clothing, movement and facial data, identified him and reconstructed his route. At 11 p.m. on 24 December officers found Phạm Ngọc Huy, 23, of Ninh Bình, at an internet café on Tô Ký street. He was a convicted thief. He confessed. Property recovery is not reported.

produced_by: Street AI cameras covering the route the intruder took, with footage retained for police review.
A model that matches people on gait, body shape, clothing and movement as well as face, so a mask does not defeat identification.
A prompt police report, the morning of the burglary, and a ward investigation team able to act on the match within hours.
must_hold: The suspect passes through camera coverage and can be found at a fixed location afterwards, here an internet café.
Identification is confirmed by police work and a confession. The sources report no independent check of the match.
The system and vendor are unnamed, so performance beyond this case cannot be checked.

later.note: The 25 December 2025 reports end with the suspect's confession and the ward police consolidating the file; no prosecution or trial report was found.

revisions.change: Record drafted from the OECD Monitor entry and five Vietnamese reports of 25 December 2025. Benefit created or restored as the classifier proposed: a post-hoc investigation that resolved a burglary, not a prevented harm. The detention time differs between outlets: Tuổi Trẻ gives 23h on 24–12, Công an nhân dân the night of 24 to 25 December, VnExpress and VietNamNet date the arrest 25 December, and Thanh Niên prints “23 giờ ngày 25.12”, which postdates its own 11:52 publication and is treated as a misprint; the date observed is 24 December. The Monitor's Pháp Luật TP.HCM link resolved only to a headline stub and is not cited; the Công an nhân dân link redirected from cand.com.vn to cand.vn when read. The victim's year of birth is 1992 (VietNamNet, CAND); the suspect's is 2002. Property recovery is not mentioned in any source; the suspect is reported to have sold the items.
Benefit type set to Reduced Violence under Trustible's full taxonomy of 23 types; it was Improved Organizational Efficiency among the six first used.
Country of the deployer added from the organization's own site or a registry.
Prose pass: a rating reason, account, purpose, the replication conditions, the system's part rewritten in shorter sentences with abbreviations expanded; facts, figures and quotations unchanged.

data.retained_case_account: Early on 23 December 2025 an intruder entered a rented room at 62 Street 51, Tân Hưng ward, Ho Chi Minh City. He took two laptops and the wallet, identity papers and bank card of the tenant, H.A.T., 33. From his account, 14 million VND was withdrawn. He reported it that morning. Tân Hưng Ward Police and the Criminal Police Division used the street AI camera system. It analyzed the masked man's gait, build, clothing, movement and facial data, identified him and reconstructed his route. At 11 p.m. on 24 December officers found Phạm Ngọc Huy, 23, of Ninh Bình, at an internet café on Tô Ký street. He was a convicted thief. He confessed. Property recovery is not reported.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: The system's contribution was identification. It matched the masked intruder's gait, body shape, clothing, movement and facial data and reconstructed his route. That pointed police to him. The detention, confession and case-building were police work. The system and its vendor are not named. No official is quoted by name. Every report draws on the police account. The OECD Monitor tags the entry under privacy and data governance and respect of human rights, the concerns that come with public facial recognition.

fields.account: Early on 23 December 2025 an intruder entered a rented room at 62 Street 51, Tân Hưng ward, Ho Chi Minh City. He took two laptops and the wallet, identity papers and bank card of the tenant, H.A.T., 33. From his account, 14 million VND was withdrawn. He reported it that morning. Tân Hưng Ward Police and the Criminal Police Division used the street AI camera system. It analyzed the masked man's gait, build, clothing, movement and facial data, identified him and reconstructed his route. At 11 p.m. on 24 December officers found Phạm Ngọc Huy, 23, of Ninh Bình, at an internet café on Tô Ký street. He was a convicted thief. He confessed. Property recovery is not reported.

Country of the deployer added from the organization's own site or a registry.

fields.account: Early on 23 December 2025 an intruder entered a rented room at 62 Street 51, Tân Hưng ward, Ho Chi Minh City. He took two laptops and the wallet, identity papers and bank card of the tenant, H.A.T., 33. From his account, 14 million VND was withdrawn. He reported it that morning. Tân Hưng Ward Police and the Criminal Police Division used the street AI camera system. It analyzed the masked man's gait, build, clothing, movement and facial data, identified him and reconstructed his route. At 11 p.m. on 24 December officers found Phạm Ngọc Huy, 23, of Ninh Bình, at an internet café on Tô Ký street. He was a convicted thief. He confessed. Property recovery is not reported.

produced_by: Street AI cameras covering the route the intruder took, with footage retained for police review.
A model that matches people on gait, body shape, clothing and movement as well as face, so a mask does not defeat identification.
A prompt police report, the morning of the burglary, and a ward investigation team able to act on the match within hours.
must_hold: The suspect passes through camera coverage and can be found at a fixed location afterwards, here an internet café.
Identification is confirmed by police work and a confession. The sources report no independent check of the match.
The system and vendor are unnamed, so performance beyond this case cannot be checked.
