record.title: GiveDirectly paid anticipatory cash in Kogi State, Nigeria, on Google Flood Hub forecast triggers (August to October 2024)
record.summary: Google Flood Hub forecast triggers paid $105 to 4,600 people in Ibaji, Kogi State, mostly before floods peaked on 21 October 2024
record.account: In 2024 GiveDirectly ran an anticipatory cash program in six wards of Ibaji, Kogi State, Nigeria. JBA Global Resilience pulled Google Flood Hub forecasts by application programming interface (API), made inundation maps and set thresholds. GiveDirectly monitored forecasts daily and cross-checked them with community observations. When 20% of a community's area was forecast to flood the trigger was met and verified residents were paid. The New Humanitarian describes an automated payout command to verified residents. GiveDirectly reports $105 to over 4,600 individuals in 53 communities. 3,250 were paid between 29 August and 6 October 2024 and 1,400 on 24 October, after floods peaked on 21 October. A $210 transfer followed. Its own survey reports weekly incomes rising from ₦4,500 to ₦10,000 and food shortages falling from 97% to 7%. A New Humanitarian investigation (31 August 2026) found data mismatches and phone-access barriers excluded some of the most vulnerable residents. GiveDirectly told the outlet it had used “household” and “individual” interchangeably. Its page note says the page was updated in July 2026, before the investigation appeared.

data.retained_case_account: In 2024 GiveDirectly ran an anticipatory cash program in six wards of Ibaji, Kogi State, Nigeria. JBA Global Resilience pulled Google Flood Hub forecasts by application programming interface (API), made inundation maps and set thresholds. GiveDirectly monitored forecasts daily and cross-checked them with community observations. When 20% of a community's area was forecast to flood the trigger was met and verified residents were paid. The New Humanitarian describes an automated payout command to verified residents. GiveDirectly reports $105 to over 4,600 individuals in 53 communities. 3,250 were paid between 29 August and 6 October 2024 and 1,400 on 24 October, after floods peaked on 21 October. A $210 transfer followed. Its own survey reports weekly incomes rising from ₦4,500 to ₦10,000 and food shortages falling from 97% to 7%. A New Humanitarian investigation (31 August 2026) found data mismatches and phone-access barriers excluded some of the most vulnerable residents. GiveDirectly told the outlet it had used “household” and “individual” interchangeably. Its page note says the page was updated in July 2026, before the investigation appeared.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: Decisive for timing and geography: GiveDirectly told The New Humanitarian that satellite/AI flood modeling determined which communities were paid and when. Individual eligibility was decided by non-AI verification (ward residence, Smile ID checks, call-center calls). The investigation identifies that as the main source of exclusions. GiveDirectly's own page attributes the late payments to identity checks in two wards.

fields.account: In 2024 GiveDirectly ran an anticipatory cash program in six wards of Ibaji, Kogi State, Nigeria. JBA Global Resilience pulled Google Flood Hub forecasts by application programming interface (API), made inundation maps and set thresholds. GiveDirectly monitored forecasts daily and cross-checked them with community observations. When 20% of a community's area was forecast to flood the trigger was met and verified residents were paid. The New Humanitarian describes an automated payout command to verified residents. GiveDirectly reports $105 to over 4,600 individuals in 53 communities. 3,250 were paid between 29 August and 6 October 2024 and 1,400 on 24 October, after floods peaked on 21 October. A $210 transfer followed. Its own survey reports weekly incomes rising from ₦4,500 to ₦10,000 and food shortages falling from 97% to 7%. A New Humanitarian investigation (31 August 2026) found data mismatches and phone-access barriers excluded some of the most vulnerable residents. GiveDirectly told the outlet it had used “household” and “individual” interchangeably. Its page note says the page was updated in July 2026, before the investigation appeared.

record.title: Xcel-funded Pano AI camera catches the Wellington fire near Breckenridge; crews hold it to one-eighth of an acre
record.summary: Xcel-funded Pano AI camera alerted crews to a campsite fire east of a Breckenridge neighborhood; firefighters said the early notice kept it to one-eighth of an acre (CBS Colorado, 9 July 2024).
record.account: CBS Colorado reported on 9 July 2024 on the Wellington fire, which broke out at an unattended campsite just east of a Breckenridge neighborhood. It was spotted by a Pano AI camera financially supported by Xcel Energy. The camera sits on a cell tower with a 360-degree view and submits an alert to emergency crews if it notices smoke. Firefighters said this was the first instance in Summit County where a wildfire was caught early thanks to the camera's early notice. It was kept to one-eighth of an acre. This followed earlier false alarms from legal campfires. Mathew Benedict of Red White and Blue Fire's Wildland Division said a location with an actual lat/long let crews drive straight to the fire. Otherwise they could spend up to an hour finding it. Xcel's Michelle Aguayo said the company had 28 Pano AI cameras installed. The fire's date is not given.

data.retained_case_account: CBS Colorado reported on 9 July 2024 on the Wellington fire, which broke out at an unattended campsite just east of a Breckenridge neighborhood. It was spotted by a Pano AI camera financially supported by Xcel Energy. The camera sits on a cell tower with a 360-degree view and submits an alert to emergency crews if it notices smoke. Firefighters said this was the first instance in Summit County where a wildfire was caught early thanks to the camera's early notice. It was kept to one-eighth of an acre. This followed earlier false alarms from legal campfires. Mathew Benedict of Red White and Blue Fire's Wildland Division said a location with an actual lat/long let crews drive straight to the fire. Otherwise they could spend up to an hour finding it. Xcel's Michelle Aguayo said the company had 28 Pano AI cameras installed. The fire's date is not given.

record.title: ALERTCalifornia AI camera alert sends Cal Fire engines to a night fire near Auburn before any 911 call
record.summary: AI camera alert at 2:33 a.m. on 6 July 2024 sent Cal Fire engines to a fire near Auburn before any 911 call; held to a 30 x 30 ft area
record.account: The ALERTCalifornia camera network is operated by UC San Diego with AI smoke-detection software from DigitalPath of Chico, California, and used by Cal Fire. It posted an alert at 2:33 a.m. on July 6 of a fire near Auburn, in the foothills east of Sacramento. The report, from September 2025, gives the day but not the year. It places the case among the previous year's fires, so 2024 is used. Nobody had called 911. Cal Fire's Grass Valley Emergency Command Center verified the alert and sent engines. Crews put the fire out before it spread beyond a 30 x 30 foot area. Cal Fire Deputy Chief Brian York said in 2024 the cameras picked up 1,668 of the 7,553 fires in Cal Fire's jurisdiction. Of those, 636 came before any person called 911.

data.retained_case_account: The ALERTCalifornia camera network is operated by UC San Diego with AI smoke-detection software from DigitalPath of Chico, California, and used by Cal Fire. It posted an alert at 2:33 a.m. on July 6 of a fire near Auburn, in the foothills east of Sacramento. The report, from September 2025, gives the day but not the year. It places the case among the previous year's fires, so 2024 is used. Nobody had called 911. Cal Fire's Grass Valley Emergency Command Center verified the alert and sent engines. Crews put the fire out before it spread beyond a 30 x 30 foot area. Cal Fire Deputy Chief Brian York said in 2024 the cameras picked up 1,668 of the 7,553 fires in Cal Fire's jurisdiction. Of those, 636 came before any person called 911.

fields.account: The ALERTCalifornia camera network is operated by UC San Diego with AI smoke-detection software from DigitalPath of Chico, California, and used by Cal Fire. It posted an alert at 2:33 a.m. on July 6 of a fire near Auburn, in the foothills east of Sacramento. The report, from September 2025, gives the day but not the year. It places the case among the previous year's fires, so 2024 is used. Nobody had called 911. Cal Fire's Grass Valley Emergency Command Center verified the alert and sent engines. Crews put the fire out before it spread beyond a 30 x 30 foot area. Cal Fire Deputy Chief Brian York said in 2024 the cameras picked up 1,668 of the 7,553 fires in Cal Fire's jurisdiction. Of those, 636 came before any person called 911.

record.title: Pano AI cameras on Xcel and CORE Electric towers spot the Bear Creek Fire; helicopters hold it to three acres
record.summary: Utility-funded Pano AI cameras detected smoke from the 16 June 2024 Bear Creek Fire in Douglas County, Colorado; helicopters were dispatched within 30 minutes and the fire was held to three acres.
record.account: On 16 June 2024 Pano AI wildfire-detection cameras on Xcel Energy and CORE Electric Cooperative towers detected smoke. It came from a lightning-caused fire in Douglas County, Colorado. According to Renewable Energy World (18 July 2024), emergency services dispatched two helicopters within 30 minutes of the identification, when the fire was 0.25 acres. The helicopters dropped 17,765 gallons of water over six hours and the fire was limited to three acres. Denver7 (17 July 2024) reported that the fire was contained within a day and was first spotted by the AI-equipped cameras. CORE's wildfire mitigation manager Jordan Ambrogi said alerts typically arrive 10 to 12 minutes after smoke is detected. The utilities, however, said the cameras identified the fire “simultaneously” with the U.S. Forest Service. So the cameras' independent contribution to containment rests on the operators' own statements (CORE interim CEO Pam Feuerstein). The OECD AI Incidents Monitor carries a separate positively framed record of Xcel's November 2023 Pano AI deployment.
record.purpose: Pano AI cameras rotate 360 degrees on mountaintop towers and use AI to detect smoke plumes. They alert utilities and fire agencies with a triangulated location. Detecting this fire early was the intended use.

data.retained_case_account: On 16 June 2024 Pano AI wildfire-detection cameras on Xcel Energy and CORE Electric Cooperative towers detected smoke. It came from a lightning-caused fire in Douglas County, Colorado. According to Renewable Energy World (18 July 2024), emergency services dispatched two helicopters within 30 minutes of the identification, when the fire was 0.25 acres. The helicopters dropped 17,765 gallons of water over six hours and the fire was limited to three acres. Denver7 (17 July 2024) reported that the fire was contained within a day and was first spotted by the AI-equipped cameras. CORE's wildfire mitigation manager Jordan Ambrogi said alerts typically arrive 10 to 12 minutes after smoke is detected. The utilities, however, said the cameras identified the fire “simultaneously” with the U.S. Forest Service. So the cameras' independent contribution to containment rests on the operators' own statements (CORE interim CEO Pam Feuerstein). The OECD AI Incidents Monitor carries a separate positively framed record of Xcel's November 2023 Pano AI deployment.

fields.account: On 16 June 2024 Pano AI wildfire-detection cameras on Xcel Energy and CORE Electric Cooperative towers detected smoke. It came from a lightning-caused fire in Douglas County, Colorado. According to Renewable Energy World (18 July 2024), emergency services dispatched two helicopters within 30 minutes of the identification, when the fire was 0.25 acres. The helicopters dropped 17,765 gallons of water over six hours and the fire was limited to three acres. Denver7 (17 July 2024) reported that the fire was contained within a day and was first spotted by the AI-equipped cameras. CORE's wildfire mitigation manager Jordan Ambrogi said alerts typically arrive 10 to 12 minutes after smoke is detected. The utilities, however, said the cameras identified the fire “simultaneously” with the U.S. Forest Service. So the cameras' independent contribution to containment rests on the operators' own statements (CORE interim CEO Pam Feuerstein). The OECD AI Incidents Monitor carries a separate positively framed record of Xcel's November 2023 Pano AI deployment.

record.summary: Cheshire Constabulary's facial recognition matched CCTV of an unknown Northwich dealer to Keenan Hughes; he and Vincent Potter were stopped on 17 May 2024 with crack cocaine and jailed on 1 July 2024.
record.account: Cheshire Constabulary's release states that in April 2024 officers in Northwich learned of a phone number used by the “Kyle” county lines gang. They recovered closed-circuit television (CCTV) of an unknown man suspected of using it. The force facial recognition system matched the image to Keenan Hughes of Connah's Quay. On Friday 17 May officers on patrol spotted Hughes on Winnington Street with Vincent Potter. A search found 99 wraps of crack cocaine worth about £990 and a hunting-style knife on Hughes. Potter had two phones, a lock knife and £960. Both pleaded guilty, and on 1 July 2024 Chester Crown Court jailed Hughes (18) for 28 months and Potter (19) for 34 months. PC Dean Butterworth said Hughes was not known locally and the technology quickly identified him as a suspect. The OECD AI Incidents Monitor records the case, listing a harm type of human or fundamental rights.

fields.account: Cheshire Constabulary's release states that in April 2024 officers in Northwich learned of a phone number used by the “Kyle” county lines gang. They recovered closed-circuit television (CCTV) of an unknown man suspected of using it. The force facial recognition system matched the image to Keenan Hughes of Connah's Quay. On Friday 17 May officers on patrol spotted Hughes on Winnington Street with Vincent Potter. A search found 99 wraps of crack cocaine worth about £990 and a hunting-style knife on Hughes. Potter had two phones, a lock knife and £960. Both pleaded guilty, and on 1 July 2024 Chester Crown Court jailed Hughes (18) for 28 months and Potter (19) for 34 months. PC Dean Butterworth said Hughes was not known locally and the technology quickly identified him as a suspect. The OECD AI Incidents Monitor records the case, listing a harm type of human or fundamental rights.

record.title: France's Foncier innovant aerial-image AI detects 140,000 undeclared pools and about €40 million in extra property tax by 20 March 2024; Dordogne alone 1,500 in 2023
record.summary: Minister Cazenave (20 March 2024): DGFiP's AI tool detected 140,000 undeclared pools, c. €40m extra property tax for local authorities; Dordogne found 1,500 in 2023. No commune-level figure found.
record.account: On 20 March 2024 Thomas Cazenave, minister for public accounts, presented the first bilan of the government's anti-fraud plan at Bercy. He said the DGFiP's algorithmic tool, Foncier innovant, introduced in October 2021, had detected 140,000 undeclared swimming pools. The tool detects pools and buildings on IGN aerial photographs and compares them with declarations. An agent then checks each detection. That would let local authorities collect about €40 million in property tax. Owners received DGFiP letters asking them to regularize (RMC, Ouest-France, L'Indépendant, 21 March 2024). CNews (11 June 2024) cites the DGFiP annual activity report as reported by Ouest-France. It gives 140,000 pools identified in 2023 and €40 million that should have been paid in 2023. That compares with 20,000 pools in the 2022 experiment in nine départements (20 Minutes). L'Indépendant instead states 120,000 for 2022, so the press accounts of the yearly split disagree. At département level, ici (France Bleu) reported on 24 March 2024 on the Dordogne public-finance office. It had found about 1,500 undeclared pools in 2023 among some 30,000 in the département. It would send property-tax catch-up notices by the end of March. No official DGFiP or ministry document is among the sources, as the ministry's website was not available. No commune-level result was found.

data.retained_case_account: On 20 March 2024 Thomas Cazenave, minister for public accounts, presented the first bilan of the government's anti-fraud plan at Bercy. He said the DGFiP's algorithmic tool, Foncier innovant, introduced in October 2021, had detected 140,000 undeclared swimming pools. The tool detects pools and buildings on IGN aerial photographs and compares them with declarations. An agent then checks each detection. That would let local authorities collect about €40 million in property tax. Owners received DGFiP letters asking them to regularize (RMC, Ouest-France, L'Indépendant, 21 March 2024). CNews (11 June 2024) cites the DGFiP annual activity report as reported by Ouest-France. It gives 140,000 pools identified in 2023 and €40 million that should have been paid in 2023. That compares with 20,000 pools in the 2022 experiment in nine départements (20 Minutes). L'Indépendant instead states 120,000 for 2022, so the press accounts of the yearly split disagree. At département level, ici (France Bleu) reported on 24 March 2024 on the Dordogne public-finance office. It had found about 1,500 undeclared pools in 2023 among some 30,000 in the département. It would send property-tax catch-up notices by the end of March. No official DGFiP or ministry document is among the sources, as the ministry's website was not available. No commune-level result was found.

fields.account: On 20 March 2024 Thomas Cazenave, minister for public accounts, presented the first bilan of the government's anti-fraud plan at Bercy. He said the DGFiP's algorithmic tool, Foncier innovant, introduced in October 2021, had detected 140,000 undeclared swimming pools. The tool detects pools and buildings on IGN aerial photographs and compares them with declarations. An agent then checks each detection. That would let local authorities collect about €40 million in property tax. Owners received DGFiP letters asking them to regularize (RMC, Ouest-France, L'Indépendant, 21 March 2024). CNews (11 June 2024) cites the DGFiP annual activity report as reported by Ouest-France. It gives 140,000 pools identified in 2023 and €40 million that should have been paid in 2023. That compares with 20,000 pools in the 2022 experiment in nine départements (20 Minutes). L'Indépendant instead states 120,000 for 2022, so the press accounts of the yearly split disagree. At département level, ici (France Bleu) reported on 24 March 2024 on the Dordogne public-finance office. It had found about 1,500 undeclared pools in 2023 among some 30,000 in the département. It would send property-tax catch-up notices by the end of March. No official DGFiP or ministry document is among the sources, as the ministry's website was not available. No commune-level result was found.

fields.summary: Minister Cazenave (20 March 2024): DGFiP's AI tool detected 140,000 undeclared pools, c. €40m extra property tax for local authorities; Dordogne found 1,500 in 2023. No commune-level figure found.
fields.account: On 20 March 2024 Thomas Cazenave, minister for public accounts, presented the first bilan of the government's anti-fraud plan at Bercy. He said the DGFiP's algorithmic tool, Foncier innovant, introduced in October 2021, had detected 140,000 undeclared swimming pools. The tool detects pools and buildings on IGN aerial photographs and compares them with declarations. An agent then checks each detection. That would let local authorities collect about €40 million in property tax. Owners received DGFiP letters asking them to regularize (RMC, Ouest-France, L'Indépendant, 21 March 2024). CNews (11 June 2024) cites the DGFiP annual activity report as reported by Ouest-France. It gives 140,000 pools identified in 2023 and €40 million that should have been paid in 2023. That compares with 20,000 pools in the 2022 experiment in nine départements (20 Minutes). L'Indépendant instead states 120,000 for 2022, so the press accounts of the yearly split disagree. At département level, ici (France Bleu) reported on 24 March 2024 on the Dordogne public-finance office. It had found about 1,500 undeclared pools in 2023 among some 30,000 in the département. It would send property-tax catch-up notices by the end of March. No official DGFiP or ministry document is among the sources, as the ministry's website was not available. No commune-level result was found.

record.title: ZeroEyes detection at Hobbs' Del Norte Pool lot leads police to people firing at clays near a street; one charged
record.summary: On 30 November 2023 ZeroEyes alerted Hobbs police to a gun on a camera at Del Norte Pool's lot; officers detained people shooting clays near a street and charged one, per the police chief.
record.account: The Odessa American (reproduced by GovTech) reports, from a ZeroEyes news release, on an alert at 6:35 p.m. MDT on 30 November 2023. ZeroEyes alerted the Hobbs Police Department and the Eagle I.C. dispatch center. A gun had been detected on a security camera in Del Norte Pool's parking lot. Those involved were shooting sporting clays close to North Grimes Street. Responding officers detained them and charges were filed against one. Hobbs Police Chief August Fons is quoted saying detection and rapid human verification helped stop the activity before anyone was hurt. Lubbock Lights later reported ZeroEyes co-founder Sam Alaimo showing images from the incident. He said it resulted in an arrest with no one hurt and listed the City of Hobbs and its school system among local clients. No court record is among the sources.

data.retained_case_account: The Odessa American (reproduced by GovTech) reports, from a ZeroEyes news release, on an alert at 6:35 p.m. MDT on 30 November 2023. ZeroEyes alerted the Hobbs Police Department and the Eagle I.C. dispatch center. A gun had been detected on a security camera in Del Norte Pool's parking lot. Those involved were shooting sporting clays close to North Grimes Street. Responding officers detained them and charges were filed against one. Hobbs Police Chief August Fons is quoted saying detection and rapid human verification helped stop the activity before anyone was hurt. Lubbock Lights later reported ZeroEyes co-founder Sam Alaimo showing images from the incident. He said it resulted in an arrest with no one hurt and listed the City of Hobbs and its school system among local clients. No court record is among the sources.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: The chain (AI detection, human verification, dispatch) is described only in ZeroEyes' release and the vendor's later interview. The chief's endorsement is quoted in that release. No police report, court filing or independent reporter observation is among the sources. The AI's necessity (whether anyone else reported the shooting) is thus undocumented.

Those involved were shooting sporting clays close to North Grimes Street. Responding officers detained them and charges were filed against one. Lubbock Lights later reported ZeroEyes co-founder Sam Alaimo showing images from the incident. He said it resulted in an arrest with no one hurt and listed the City of Hobbs and its school system among local clients. No court record is among the sources.

record.title: LAPD's Boston Dynamics Spot quadruped is sent onto a Hollywood Metro bus during a two-hour standoff with an armed man found asleep; he wakes, surrenders and is arrested, and the gun proves to be a BB gun
record.summary: LAPD deployed its Boston Dynamics Spot quadruped during a 8 November 2023 standoff with an armed man asleep on a Hollywood Metro bus; he woke, surrendered and was arrested; the gun was a BB gun.
record.account: Just before 4 a.m. on 8 November 2023, a passenger on a Metro bus in Hollywood reported an armed man aboard. The bus was at Melrose and Western avenues. The driver pulled over and evacuated the other passengers. Officers got no response from the man, and a two-hour standoff followed (Los Angeles Times via Police1, 9 November 2023). The LAPD sent in its Boston Dynamics Spot quadruped. Its camera confirmed the man was asleep with a gun (Police1). The LAPD's quarterly report to the Police Commission says the robot was a barrier between suspect and firearm (NBC Los Angeles, 8 March 2024). The man woke, left the bus and was taken into custody about 6:40 a.m. The weapon was a BB gun (Police1). Deputy Chief David Kowalski approves each use. The robot cost nearly $300,000 (NBC). International Business Times' October 2024 account says the robot removed the gun.

record.taxonomy_note: Trustible's Reduced Violence covers a weapon found, but what the sources establish is that officers kept their distance while a camera confirmed a sleeping, apparently armed man and the gun proved to be a BB gun; the good is the lowered risk to officers and the public while the standoff ran.

ratings.reason: The LAPD could confirm from the robot's camera that the man was asleep. By its own report, it kept the robot between him and the gun. The two-hour standoff ended in an arrest with no injury reported. A measurable result for the unit, with no counterfactual that officers would otherwise have been hurt.

The passengers had been evacuated before the robot was used, and the suspect was taken into custody unharmed. None of the reports ties either outcome to the robot rather than to the man waking and leaving the bus.

fields.account: Just before 4 a.m. on 8 November 2023, a passenger on a Metro bus in Hollywood reported an armed man aboard. The bus was at Melrose and Western avenues. The driver pulled over and evacuated the other passengers. Officers got no response from the man, and a two-hour standoff followed (Los Angeles Times via Police1, 9 November 2023). The LAPD sent in its Boston Dynamics Spot quadruped. Its camera confirmed the man was asleep with a gun (Police1). The LAPD's quarterly report to the Police Commission says the robot was a barrier between suspect and firearm (NBC Los Angeles, 8 March 2024). The man woke, left the bus and was taken into custody about 6:40 a.m. The weapon was a BB gun (Police1). Deputy Chief David Kowalski approves each use. The robot cost nearly $300,000 (NBC). International Business Times' October 2024 account says the robot removed the gun.

ratings.reason: The LAPD could confirm from the robot's camera that the man was asleep. By its own report, it kept the robot between him and the gun. The two-hour standoff ended in an arrest with no injury reported. A measurable result for the unit, with no counterfactual that officers would otherwise have been hurt.

The passengers had been evacuated before the robot was used, and the suspect was taken into custody unharmed. None of the reports ties either outcome to the robot rather than to the man waking and leaving the bus.

fields.summary: LAPD deployed its Boston Dynamics Spot quadruped during a 8 November 2023 standoff with an armed man asleep on a Hollywood Metro bus; he woke, surrendered and was arrested; the gun was a BB gun.
fields.account: Just before 4 a.m. on 8 November 2023, a passenger on a Metro bus in Hollywood reported an armed man aboard. The bus was at Melrose and Western avenues. The driver pulled over and evacuated the other passengers. Officers got no response from the man, and a two-hour standoff followed (Los Angeles Times via Police1, 9 November 2023). The LAPD sent in its Boston Dynamics Spot quadruped. Its camera confirmed the man was asleep with a gun (Police1). The LAPD's quarterly report to the Police Commission says the robot was a barrier between suspect and firearm (NBC Los Angeles, 8 March 2024). The man woke, left the bus and was taken into custody about 6:40 a.m. The weapon was a BB gun (Police1). Deputy Chief David Kowalski approves each use. The robot cost nearly $300,000 (NBC). International Business Times' October 2024 account says the robot removed the gun.

record.title: ALERTCalifornia's AI flags a 3 am smoke column near Mount Laguna; human operators verify it and Cal Fire holds the fire to under a quarter acre
record.summary: AI on Cleveland National Forest cameras flagged smoke at about 3 am on 5 August 2023; Cal Fire held the verified fire under a quarter acre.
record.account: At about 3 am on 5 August 2023, the ALERTCalifornia AI flagged a column of smoke in the Cleveland National Forest near Mount Laguna. That is about 40 miles east of San Diego. The AI, a machine-learned model run by UC San Diego, watches live feeds from more than 1,000 cameras. Human operators verified the detection and alerted Cal Fire Captain Kris Yeary. His crews put it out at less than a quarter acre. Yeary told AFP that it could have become a devastating fire had the AI not alerted them. The AI watch over the feeds began at the end of June 2023 under a Cal Fire trial. By September 2023 the tool reached all 21 Cal Fire dispatch centers.

data.retained_case_account: At about 3 am on 5 August 2023, the ALERTCalifornia AI flagged a column of smoke in the Cleveland National Forest near Mount Laguna. That is about 40 miles east of San Diego. The AI, a machine-learned model run by UC San Diego, watches live feeds from more than 1,000 cameras. Human operators verified the detection and alerted Cal Fire Captain Kris Yeary. His crews put it out at less than a quarter acre. Yeary told AFP that it could have become a devastating fire had the AI not alerted them. The AI watch over the feeds began at the end of June 2023 under a Cal Fire trial. By September 2023 the tool reached all 21 Cal Fire dispatch centers.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: The model's contribution was the detection. Its algorithm flagged a smoke column in a Cleveland National Forest camera feed at about 3 am. Human operators verified it before Cal Fire was alerted. The containment was done by Captain Yeary's crews. No source records whether a 911 call would have come later. The time gained is documented only for the program as a whole. TIME reports 77 fires identified before any 911 call in the first two months. UC San Diego's Neal Driscoll says the alerts beat 911 calls about 40 percent of the time. AFP also notes the system sometimes misreads dust, insects or weather as smoke. That is why the human verification step sits between the model and the dispatch.

fields.account: At about 3 am on 5 August 2023, the ALERTCalifornia AI flagged a column of smoke in the Cleveland National Forest near Mount Laguna. That is about 40 miles east of San Diego. The AI, a machine-learned model run by UC San Diego, watches live feeds from more than 1,000 cameras. Human operators verified the detection and alerted Cal Fire Captain Kris Yeary. His crews put it out at less than a quarter acre. Yeary told AFP that it could have become a devastating fire had the AI not alerted them. The AI watch over the feeds began at the end of June 2023 under a Cal Fire trial. By September 2023 the tool reached all 21 Cal Fire dispatch centers.

record.title: xView2 machine-learning damage maps may have been used by UN INSARAG teams in Adıyaman and by AFAD, the World Bank, IFRC and WFP after the 6 February 2023 Türkiye earthquakes
record.summary: MIT Technology Review (20 February 2023), quoting DIU: xView2 used by two UN INSARAG teams in Adıyaman and by AFAD, World Bank, IFRC and WFP; Microsoft reports 3,849 damaged buildings mapped for AFAD.
record.account: MIT Technology Review reported on 20 February 2023 on xView2, an open-source building-damage assessment project. It was sponsored and developed in 2019 by the Pentagon's Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) and Carnegie Mellon University's Software Engineering Institute. Partners included Microsoft and UC Berkeley. It uses machine-learning (semantic segmentation) on satellite imagery to identify and grade building damage. Ritwik Gupta, DIU's principal AI scientist, told the magazine about use in Türkiye. At least two ground teams of search and rescue personnel from the UN's International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG) had used xView2 in Adıyaman. He said it helped workers find damaged areas they were unaware of. He said AFAD, the World Bank, the IFRC and WFP had all used the platform. Atishay Abbhi, a World Bank disaster risk management specialist, said the same degree of assessment would typically take weeks and now takes hours or minutes. The article notes that the first usable satellite images came on 9 February 2023, three days after the first quake. It says the model is up to 85 or 90% accurate. Microsoft's February 2023 “Turkey Earthquake Report” has authors including Gupta and Microsoft AI for Good staff. It states that the team partnered with AFAD to deliver building-level damage estimates over four cities in southeast Türkiye. The imagery was from the first three days. It estimated 3,849 buildings damaged or destroyed, with Marash the most affected at 7.44% of buildings. The World Bank GRADE report does not mention xView2, AI or Microsoft. DLR's peer-reviewed account states its own AI damage products were not part of the viewer delivered to responders. Direct Relief's December 2025 article describes a research study on Microsoft and Google models rather than a response decision. No responder statement describing a decision taken on xView2 output is among the sources.

data.retained_case_account: MIT Technology Review reported on 20 February 2023 on xView2, an open-source building-damage assessment project. It was sponsored and developed in 2019 by the Pentagon's Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) and Carnegie Mellon University's Software Engineering Institute. Partners included Microsoft and UC Berkeley. It uses machine-learning (semantic segmentation) on satellite imagery to identify and grade building damage. Ritwik Gupta, DIU's principal AI scientist, told the magazine about use in Türkiye. At least two ground teams of search and rescue personnel from the UN's International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG) had used xView2 in Adıyaman. He said it helped workers find damaged areas they were unaware of. He said AFAD, the World Bank, the IFRC and WFP had all used the platform. Atishay Abbhi, a World Bank disaster risk management specialist, said the same degree of assessment would typically take weeks and now takes hours or minutes. The article notes that the first usable satellite images came on 9 February 2023, three days after the first quake. It says the model is up to 85 or 90% accurate. Microsoft's February 2023 “Turkey Earthquake Report” has authors including Gupta and Microsoft AI for Good staff. It states that the team partnered with AFAD to deliver building-level damage estimates over four cities in southeast Türkiye. The imagery was from the first three days. It estimated 3,849 buildings damaged or destroyed, with Marash the most affected at 7.44% of buildings. The World Bank GRADE report does not mention xView2, AI or Microsoft. DLR's peer-reviewed account states its own AI damage products were not part of the viewer delivered to responders. Direct Relief's December 2025 article describes a research study on Microsoft and Google models rather than a response decision. No responder statement describing a decision taken on xView2 output is among the sources.

fields.account: MIT Technology Review reported on 20 February 2023 on xView2, an open-source building-damage assessment project. It was sponsored and developed in 2019 by the Pentagon's Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) and Carnegie Mellon University's Software Engineering Institute. Partners included Microsoft and UC Berkeley. It uses machine-learning (semantic segmentation) on satellite imagery to identify and grade building damage. Ritwik Gupta, DIU's principal AI scientist, told the magazine about use in Türkiye. At least two ground teams of search and rescue personnel from the UN's International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG) had used xView2 in Adıyaman. He said it helped workers find damaged areas they were unaware of. He said AFAD, the World Bank, the IFRC and WFP had all used the platform. Atishay Abbhi, a World Bank disaster risk management specialist, said the same degree of assessment would typically take weeks and now takes hours or minutes. The article notes that the first usable satellite images came on 9 February 2023, three days after the first quake. It says the model is up to 85 or 90% accurate. Microsoft's February 2023 “Turkey Earthquake Report” has authors including Gupta and Microsoft AI for Good staff. It states that the team partnered with AFAD to deliver building-level damage estimates over four cities in southeast Türkiye. The imagery was from the first three days. It estimated 3,849 buildings damaged or destroyed, with Marash the most affected at 7.44% of buildings. The World Bank GRADE report does not mention xView2, AI or Microsoft. DLR's peer-reviewed account states its own AI damage products were not part of the viewer delivered to responders. Direct Relief's December 2025 article describes a research study on Microsoft and Google models rather than a response decision. No responder statement describing a decision taken on xView2 output is among the sources.

fields.account: MIT Technology Review reported on 20 February 2023 on xView2, an open-source building-damage assessment project. It was sponsored and developed in 2019 by the Pentagon's Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) and Carnegie Mellon University's Software Engineering Institute. Partners included Microsoft and UC Berkeley. It uses machine-learning (semantic segmentation) on satellite imagery to identify and grade building damage. Ritwik Gupta, DIU's principal AI scientist, told the magazine about use in Türkiye. At least two ground teams of search and rescue personnel from the UN's International Search and Rescue Advisory Group (INSARAG) had used xView2 in Adıyaman. He said it helped workers find damaged areas they were unaware of. He said AFAD, the World Bank, the IFRC and WFP had all used the platform. Atishay Abbhi, a World Bank disaster risk management specialist, said the same degree of assessment would typically take weeks and now takes hours or minutes. The article notes that the first usable satellite images came on 9 February 2023, three days after the first quake. It says the model is up to 85 or 90% accurate. Microsoft's February 2023 “Turkey Earthquake Report” has authors including Gupta and Microsoft AI for Good staff. It states that the team partnered with AFAD to deliver building-level damage estimates over four cities in southeast Türkiye. The imagery was from the first three days. It estimated 3,849 buildings damaged or destroyed, with Marash the most affected at 7.44% of buildings. The World Bank GRADE report does not mention xView2, AI or Microsoft. DLR's peer-reviewed account states its own AI damage products were not part of the viewer delivered to responders. Direct Relief's December 2025 article describes a research study on Microsoft and Google models rather than a response decision. No responder statement describing a decision taken on xView2 output is among the sources.

record.title: Instagram self-harm alert to Madhya Pradesh cyber police leads Satna officers to a 17-year-old within about an hour; she is counseled and sent home (3 November 2022)
record.summary: 3 November 2022, about 5 pm: Instagram emailed MP cyber police a self-harm alert; Bhopal and Indore teams traced a 17-year-old to Satna in about an hour; she was counseled and sent home.
record.account: On 3 November 2022 at about 5 pm, Madhya Pradesh's state cyber police received an alert emailed by Instagram's US office. It said a user in the state had suffered a body injury. The Indore cyber-crime unit shared the “self-harm” alert with the cyber headquarters in Bhopal (ANI, 5 November 2022; Times of India, 4 November 2022). The girl, 17, had uploaded two videos. In one, a packet of poison lay beside her as she acted as if drunk. In the other she appeared to cut a vein (ANI). The Times of India notes a small cut on her wrist. State Cyber SP Vaibhav Shrivastava said: “After an effort of one hour, we traced the location of the girl”. She was in Satna district, whose police were informed (ANI). Satna SP Ashutosh Gupta said officers located her and called her in with her mother. She said she only wanted to scare her boyfriend and was sent home after counseling (Times of India).

fields.account: On 3 November 2022 at about 5 pm, Madhya Pradesh's state cyber police received an alert emailed by Instagram's US office. It said a user in the state had suffered a body injury. The Indore cyber-crime unit shared the “self-harm” alert with the cyber headquarters in Bhopal (ANI, 5 November 2022; Times of India, 4 November 2022). The girl, 17, had uploaded two videos. In one, a packet of poison lay beside her as she acted as if drunk. In the other she appeared to cut a vein (ANI). The Times of India notes a small cut on her wrist. State Cyber SP Vaibhav Shrivastava said: “After an effort of one hour, we traced the location of the girl”. She was in Satna district, whose police were informed (ANI). Satna SP Ashutosh Gupta said officers located her and called her in with her mother. She said she only wanted to scare her boyfriend and was sent home after counseling (Times of India).

fields.account: On 3 November 2022 at about 5 pm, Madhya Pradesh's state cyber police received an alert emailed by Instagram's US office. It said a user in the state had suffered a body injury. The Indore cyber-crime unit shared the “self-harm” alert with the cyber headquarters in Bhopal (ANI, 5 November 2022; Times of India, 4 November 2022). The girl, 17, had uploaded two videos. In one, a packet of poison lay beside her as she acted as if drunk. In the other she appeared to cut a vein (ANI). The Times of India notes a small cut on her wrist. State Cyber SP Vaibhav Shrivastava said: “After an effort of one hour, we traced the location of the girl”. She was in Satna district, whose police were informed (ANI). Satna SP Ashutosh Gupta said officers located her and called her in with her mother. She said she only wanted to scare her boyfriend and was sent home after counseling (Times of India).

record.summary: NRW Interior Ministry, 28 Oct 2022: Palantir-based DAR resolved an amok-threat email against Siegen's city administration in seconds and identified 51 of about 100 people at a Duisburg clan shooting.
record.account: On 28 October 2022 North Rhine-Westphalia's (NRW) Interior Ministry said DAR, the police's Palantir software, was central in several recent cases (WELT; RP Online). In October someone had emailed the Siegen city administration announcing an amok attack. The threat was over the city's “topless” permission for swimming pools. The ministry said the email address revealed the suspect via Palantir in fractions of a second. A shooting in Duisburg-Hamborn between a Turkish-Arab clan and the Hells Angels injured four people. A Duisburg investigator said police quickly identified 51 of the roughly 100 participants, about 20 minutes each (RP Online; WELT). 49 of them were assigned to rival groups. Interior Minister Herbert Reul addressed the Landtag's interior committee on 27 October. He said DAR links the weapons register, residents' registration, the police case system and the wanted-persons portal. The ministry puts the 2019–2025 cost at about 39 million euros. The opposition attacks it on data-protection and cost grounds (WELT).

fields.account: On 28 October 2022 North Rhine-Westphalia's (NRW) Interior Ministry said DAR, the police's Palantir software, was central in several recent cases (WELT; RP Online). In October someone had emailed the Siegen city administration announcing an amok attack. The threat was over the city's “topless” permission for swimming pools. The ministry said the email address revealed the suspect via Palantir in fractions of a second. A shooting in Duisburg-Hamborn between a Turkish-Arab clan and the Hells Angels injured four people. A Duisburg investigator said police quickly identified 51 of the roughly 100 participants, about 20 minutes each (RP Online; WELT). 49 of them were assigned to rival groups. Interior Minister Herbert Reul addressed the Landtag's interior committee on 27 October. He said DAR links the weapons register, residents' registration, the police case system and the wanted-persons portal. The ministry puts the 2019–2025 cost at about 39 million euros. The opposition attacks it on data-protection and cost grounds (WELT).

fields.summary: NRW Interior Ministry, 28 Oct 2022: Palantir-based DAR resolved an amok-threat email against Siegen's city administration in seconds and identified 51 of about 100 people at a Duisburg clan shooting.
fields.account: On 28 October 2022 North Rhine-Westphalia's (NRW) Interior Ministry said DAR, the police's Palantir software, was central in several recent cases (WELT; RP Online). In October someone had emailed the Siegen city administration announcing an amok attack. The threat was over the city's “topless” permission for swimming pools. The ministry said the email address revealed the suspect via Palantir in fractions of a second. A shooting in Duisburg-Hamborn between a Turkish-Arab clan and the Hells Angels injured four people. A Duisburg investigator said police quickly identified 51 of the roughly 100 participants, about 20 minutes each (RP Online; WELT). 49 of them were assigned to rival groups. Interior Minister Herbert Reul addressed the Landtag's interior committee on 27 October. He said DAR links the weapons register, residents' registration, the police case system and the wanted-persons portal. The ministry puts the 2019–2025 cost at about 39 million euros. The opposition attacks it on data-protection and cost grounds (WELT).

record.title: Westchester County police use Rekor plate-reader pattern analysis to stop David Zayas in Scarsdale; crack cocaine, cash and a pistol found and he is convicted
record.summary: Westchester County PD's Rekor system flagged David Zayas's driving pattern across 480 cameras; a March 2022 stop in Scarsdale found crack cocaine, cash and a pistol; he was convicted (Carscoops).
record.account: Carscoops reports that the Westchester County Police Department, New York, used technology provided by Rekor. It examined the driving patterns of anyone passing its 480 license-plate-reader cameras over a two-year period. It determined that David Zayas had made several trips along routes typically used by drug traffickers and turned around quickly to go home. In March 2022 Zayas was driving a gray Chevrolet in Scarsdale. Officers pulled him over, searched the car and found crack cocaine, cash and a pistol. The case ended in his conviction (Carscoops, 18 July 2023, drawing on Forbes). The Star's AFP Relaxnews item adds that police took an interest in a vehicle registered to Zayas in March 2022. The OECD Monitor summary says the system analyzed billions of plate records and lists rights and public-interest harms. Carscoops quotes ACLU lawyer Brett Max Kaufman and defense attorney Ben Gold criticizing the surveillance. Only the month is given, so 1 March 2022 is used.

data.retained_case_account: Carscoops reports that the Westchester County Police Department, New York, used technology provided by Rekor. It examined the driving patterns of anyone passing its 480 license-plate-reader cameras over a two-year period. It determined that David Zayas had made several trips along routes typically used by drug traffickers and turned around quickly to go home. In March 2022 Zayas was driving a gray Chevrolet in Scarsdale. Officers pulled him over, searched the car and found crack cocaine, cash and a pistol. The case ended in his conviction (Carscoops, 18 July 2023, drawing on Forbes). The Star's AFP Relaxnews item adds that police took an interest in a vehicle registered to Zayas in March 2022. The OECD Monitor summary says the system analyzed billions of plate records and lists rights and public-interest harms. Carscoops quotes ACLU lawyer Brett Max Kaufman and defense attorney Ben Gold criticizing the surveillance. Only the month is given, so 1 March 2022 is used.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: Per Carscoops, Rekor-supplied analysis over 480 cameras and two years of reads produced the ground for the stop. That was several trips on routes typically used by drug traffickers with quick turnarounds. Everything after the flag was police work; the conviction rested on what the search found. The original Forbes report, which cited court filings, is not among the sources. The sources on record give no accuracy figure, no count of other flagged drivers and no court ruling on the stop. Carscoops quotes Ben Gold calling avoidance of the system unfeasible and Brett Max Kaufman calling the surveillance's scale massive.

fields.account: Carscoops reports that the Westchester County Police Department, New York, used technology provided by Rekor. It examined the driving patterns of anyone passing its 480 license-plate-reader cameras over a two-year period. It determined that David Zayas had made several trips along routes typically used by drug traffickers and turned around quickly to go home. In March 2022 Zayas was driving a gray Chevrolet in Scarsdale. Officers pulled him over, searched the car and found crack cocaine, cash and a pistol. The case ended in his conviction (Carscoops, 18 July 2023, drawing on Forbes). The Star's AFP Relaxnews item adds that police took an interest in a vehicle registered to Zayas in March 2022. The OECD Monitor summary says the system analyzed billions of plate records and lists rights and public-interest harms. Carscoops quotes ACLU lawyer Brett Max Kaufman and defense attorney Ben Gold criticizing the surveillance. Only the month is given, so 1 March 2022 is used.

record.account: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority's report “AML/CFT Regtech: Case Studies and Insights” (January 2021; press release 21 January 2021) presents anonymized bank case studies. Bank F is a subsidiary and regional head office of a large global bank in Asia-Pacific, per the report. It implemented a network (graph) analytics solution in Hong Kong in 2013. It identified high-risk customers and transactions from wholesale client, correspondent banking, trade, payments and external registry data. In a 2015 example, a relationship manager gathered intelligence about trade-based money laundering (TBML) related to a drug cartel in one account. The manager linked it to a second account via the CRM tool. The tool then identified additional companies linked to the first two parties through linked phone numbers and email addresses. Account reviews for Companies A, B and C revealed potential money laundering concerns. The report states that by 2016 Bank F covered its top 20 commercial banking sites and about 80% of its trade lending book. The tool has led to review of around 100 customer relationships holding around USD 500 million in clean or unsecured exposures, it says. The report’s USD 50 million figure assumes that 10% of those exposures would otherwise be unrecoverable. It does not document USD 50 million in realized savings. The foreword adds that such techniques are already neutralizing mule account networks linked to face mask scams. The 2015 example carries no day.

It identified high-risk customers and transactions from wholesale client, correspondent banking, trade, payments and external registry data. In a 2015 example, a relationship manager gathered intelligence about trade-based money laundering (TBML) related to a drug cartel in one account. The manager linked it to a second account via the CRM tool. The tool then identified additional companies linked to the first two parties through linked phone numbers and email addresses. Account reviews for Companies A, B and C revealed potential money laundering concerns. The report states that by 2016 Bank F covered its top 20 commercial banking sites and about 80% of its trade lending book. The tool has led to review of around 100 customer relationships holding around USD 500 million in clean or unsecured exposures, it says. The report’s USD 50 million figure assumes that 10% of those exposures would otherwise be unrecoverable. It does not document USD 50 million in realized savings. The foreword adds that such techniques are already neutralizing mule account networks linked to face mask scams. The 2015 example carries no day.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: The HKMA report attributes the identification of Company C to the network analytics tool's matching of linked phone numbers and email addresses. A human relationship manager supplied the initial lead. Whether the tool uses machine learning is not stated. The bank built and deployed the tool itself. The HKMA, which wrote the report, is the regulator.

fields.summary: Bank F’s network tool found phone numbers and email addresses shared by three companies. Further account checks indicated possible money laundering.
fields.account: The Hong Kong Monetary Authority's report “AML/CFT Regtech: Case Studies and Insights” (January 2021; press release 21 January 2021) presents anonymized bank case studies. Bank F is a subsidiary and regional head office of a large global bank in Asia-Pacific, per the report. It implemented a network (graph) analytics solution in Hong Kong in 2013. It identified high-risk customers and transactions from wholesale client, correspondent banking, trade, payments and external registry data. In a 2015 example, a relationship manager gathered intelligence about trade-based money laundering (TBML) related to a drug cartel in one account. The manager linked it to a second account via the CRM tool. The tool then identified additional companies linked to the first two parties through linked phone numbers and email addresses. Account reviews for Companies A, B and C revealed potential money laundering concerns. The report states that by 2016 Bank F covered its top 20 commercial banking sites and about 80% of its trade lending book. The tool has led to review of around 100 customer relationships holding around USD 500 million in clean or unsecured exposures, it says. The report’s USD 50 million figure assumes that 10% of those exposures would otherwise be unrecoverable. It does not document USD 50 million in realized savings. The foreword adds that such techniques are already neutralizing mule account networks linked to face mask scams. The 2015 example carries no day.

record.summary: CBP's new facial comparison system at Dulles reported a mismatch for a man presenting a French passport on 22 August 2018; a Congolese ID was found in his shoe and he was returned to Brazil.
record.account: On 22 August 2018, the third day of facial comparison biometrics at Washington Dulles International Airport, a 26-year-old man arrived from Sao Paulo. He presented a French passport at primary inspection. CBP's release states the officer used the facial comparison biometric technology, which confirmed the man was not a match to the passport. In secondary inspection officers found his authentic Republic of Congo identification card concealed in his shoe. CBP Area Port Director Daniel Mattina told NBC News the man was apprehended, processed and returned to Brazil. CBP called him the first impostor detected with the technology. CBP releases record a second (8 September 2018) and third (1 October 2018) impostor at Dulles and, by September 2021, more than 900 impostors nationally. The sources do not name the matching-algorithm vendor.

fields.account: On 22 August 2018, the third day of facial comparison biometrics at Washington Dulles International Airport, a 26-year-old man arrived from Sao Paulo. He presented a French passport at primary inspection. CBP's release states the officer used the facial comparison biometric technology, which confirmed the man was not a match to the passport. In secondary inspection officers found his authentic Republic of Congo identification card concealed in his shoe. CBP Area Port Director Daniel Mattina told NBC News the man was apprehended, processed and returned to Brazil. CBP called him the first impostor detected with the technology. CBP releases record a second (8 September 2018) and third (1 October 2018) impostor at Dulles and, by September 2021, more than 900 impostors nationally. The sources do not name the matching-algorithm vendor.

fields.summary: CBP's new facial comparison system at Dulles reported a mismatch for a man presenting a French passport on 22 August 2018; a Congolese ID was found in his shoe and he was returned to Brazil.
fields.account: On 22 August 2018, the third day of facial comparison biometrics at Washington Dulles International Airport, a 26-year-old man arrived from Sao Paulo. He presented a French passport at primary inspection. CBP's release states the officer used the facial comparison biometric technology, which confirmed the man was not a match to the passport. In secondary inspection officers found his authentic Republic of Congo identification card concealed in his shoe. CBP Area Port Director Daniel Mattina told NBC News the man was apprehended, processed and returned to Brazil. CBP called him the first impostor detected with the technology. CBP releases record a second (8 September 2018) and third (1 October 2018) impostor at Dulles and, by September 2021, more than 900 impostors nationally. The sources do not name the matching-algorithm vendor.

details.label: Purpose
details.value: Anthropic's consumer terms (effective 8 October 2025) reserve the right “at our sole discretion” to report Inputs to law enforcement. Its privacy policy (effective 10 September 2026) allows disclosure the company believes “reasonably necessary” to “prevent serious harm to any person or to property”. The arrest report says the platform's safety measures are “designed to monitor for key phrases and potentially threatening content”. Flagging a stated shooting threat, reviewing it by hand and referring it to police was that purpose. Of an August 2026 referral Anthropic said “This is our safeguards process working as intended”.

details.label: AI contribution
details.value: The arrest report says the platform “utilizes safety and security measures designed to monitor for key phrases and potentially threatening content”. It says the messages were “escalated to a human review team”. An automated layer therefore surfaced the two messages, and people judged their severity and made the referral. The sources do not say whether the flag came from a classifier or a keyword rule. Straight Arrow News, citing court records, says the review team escalated to the FBI, which notified the sheriff's office. Identifying the user, the home visit, the Miranda interview and the charging decision were the work of Lee County deputies and Intelligence Detective Thomas Alejo. The arrest report calls the platform “Anthropic Artificial Intelligence”. Press reports name Claude, and court records note the user told the detective she used Perplexity.

record.title: Anthropic's threat monitoring flags a Bonita Springs woman's messages about shooting up the Lee County Sheriff's Office; human reviewers tip police, who detain her without incident and find no gun
record.summary: Anthropic safeguards flagged a threat to shoot up a Florida sheriff's office; reviewers tipped police, who arrested the user; no gun found.
record.account: A user of Anthropic's AI chat service wrote at about 05:10 on 26 September 2026. She said she was going to “shoot up” the Lee County Sheriff's Office in Florida. At 01:07 on 27 September she wrote that she had got a new gun. Anthropic's safety monitoring flagged the messages, and because of their severity a human review team reported them to law enforcement. The sheriff's office logged the tip on 29 September and identified the user as Carli Michelle Heller, 30, of Bonita Springs. Deputies detained her at home without incident at 00:51 on 30 September. A detective charged her under Florida Statute 836.10, written threats of violence. No weapon was seized, and she described the AI as a personal diary.

produced_by: A vendor practice of screening consumer chats for threatening content and escalating severe cases to a human review team. That team can refer them to law enforcement, which Anthropic's consumer terms and privacy policy permit
A tip carrying enough account information for the sheriff's office to identify a named resident within days
A local agency that treated a stated threat against its own building as credible enough to send deputies the same night
must_hold: The referral must identify a real person and a real risk. The Lee County Sheriff's Office told reporters it does not count tips from Anthropic. No public figures exist on how often such referrals are made or prove unfounded

The disclosure must stay within the emergency exception of the Stored Communications Act. An EFF attorney told Straight Arrow News “there is always the risk of over-reporting”, and the Monitor logs reputational and psychological harm to the user

The response must remain proportionate. Here no weapon was found, and the user described a personal diary. Whether a chatbot prompt is a punishable threat under Florida Statute 836.10 is contested by the defense and by Eugene Volokh

The attribution to Claude rests on press reports and the arrest report's phrase “Anthropic Artificial Intelligence”. Court records also note the user told the detective she used Perplexity, and her attorney declined to say which

data.retained_case_account: A user of Anthropic's AI chat service wrote at about 05:10 on 26 September 2026. She said she was going to “shoot up” the Lee County Sheriff's Office in Florida. At 01:07 on 27 September she wrote that she had got a new gun. Anthropic's safety monitoring flagged the messages, and because of their severity a human review team reported them to law enforcement. The sheriff's office logged the tip on 29 September and identified the user as Carli Michelle Heller, 30, of Bonita Springs. Deputies detained her at home without incident at 00:51 on 30 September. A detective charged her under Florida Statute 836.10, written threats of violence. No weapon was seized, and she described the AI as a personal diary.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: The arrest report says the platform “utilizes safety and security measures designed to monitor for key phrases and potentially threatening content”. It says the messages were “escalated to a human review team”. An automated layer therefore surfaced the two messages, and people judged their severity and made the referral. The sources do not say whether the flag came from a classifier or a keyword rule. Straight Arrow News, citing court records, says the review team escalated to the FBI, which notified the sheriff's office. Identifying the user, the home visit, the Miranda interview and the charging decision were the work of Lee County deputies and Intelligence Detective Thomas Alejo. The arrest report calls the platform “Anthropic Artificial Intelligence”. Press reports name Claude, and court records note the user told the detective she used Perplexity.

fields.summary: Anthropic safeguards flagged a threat to shoot up a Florida sheriff's office; reviewers tipped police, who arrested the user; no gun found.
fields.account: A user of Anthropic's AI chat service wrote at about 05:10 on 26 September 2026. She said she was going to “shoot up” the Lee County Sheriff's Office in Florida. At 01:07 on 27 September she wrote that she had got a new gun. Anthropic's safety monitoring flagged the messages, and because of their severity a human review team reported them to law enforcement. The sheriff's office logged the tip on 29 September and identified the user as Carli Michelle Heller, 30, of Bonita Springs. Deputies detained her at home without incident at 00:51 on 30 September. A detective charged her under Florida Statute 836.10, written threats of violence. No weapon was seized, and she described the AI as a personal diary.

record.summary: SETN (21 Jan 2026, citing Japanese media): the helicopter took off at 10:52 on 20 Jan 2026 and lost contact at 11:04; the fire department had already received a collision notification from a passen...
record.account: Taiwan's SETN reported on 21 Jan 2026, citing Japanese media, on a sightseeing helicopter operated by Aso Cadre Dominion. It carried a pilot in his sixties and two Taiwanese passengers (a 41-year-old man and a 36-year-old woman). It took off at 10:52 Japan time on 20 Jan 2026 and lost contact at 11:04. Before contact was lost, the local fire department received a “strong impact” notification from a passenger's phone, apparently the iPhone Crash Detection feature. Callbacks to the phone failed. An object believed to be the helicopter was found around the first crater of Mount Aso's Nakadake. The article does not state the fate of the three occupants. It does not cite a named Japanese agency. It quotes a firefighter and a nurse on crash detection in general. Apple's feature, on iPhone 14 and later, uses motion sensors and an on-device algorithm to call emergency services after a 10-second countdown. The OECD AI Incidents Monitor lists the case as a protective response. The link to transport safety is indirect. The device alerted responders to an aviation crash it did not prevent.

data.retained_case_account: Taiwan's SETN reported on 21 Jan 2026, citing Japanese media, on a sightseeing helicopter operated by Aso Cadre Dominion. It carried a pilot in his sixties and two Taiwanese passengers (a 41-year-old man and a 36-year-old woman). It took off at 10:52 Japan time on 20 Jan 2026 and lost contact at 11:04. Before contact was lost, the local fire department received a “strong impact” notification from a passenger's phone, apparently the iPhone Crash Detection feature. Callbacks to the phone failed. An object believed to be the helicopter was found around the first crater of Mount Aso's Nakadake. The article does not state the fate of the three occupants. It does not cite a named Japanese agency. It quotes a firefighter and a nurse on crash detection in general. Apple's feature, on iPhone 14 and later, uses motion sensors and an on-device algorithm to call emergency services after a 10-second countdown. The OECD AI Incidents Monitor lists the case as a protective response. The link to transport safety is indirect. The device alerted responders to an aviation crash it did not prevent.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: The phone's crash algorithm sent the notification. The search located the wreckage the following day. The cited source does not say the alert's coordinates guided it or that anyone was rescued alive.

fields.account: Taiwan's SETN reported on 21 Jan 2026, citing Japanese media, on a sightseeing helicopter operated by Aso Cadre Dominion. It carried a pilot in his sixties and two Taiwanese passengers (a 41-year-old man and a 36-year-old woman). It took off at 10:52 Japan time on 20 Jan 2026 and lost contact at 11:04. Before contact was lost, the local fire department received a “strong impact” notification from a passenger's phone, apparently the iPhone Crash Detection feature. Callbacks to the phone failed. An object believed to be the helicopter was found around the first crater of Mount Aso's Nakadake. The article does not state the fate of the three occupants. It does not cite a named Japanese agency. It quotes a firefighter and a nurse on crash detection in general. Apple's feature, on iPhone 14 and later, uses motion sensors and an on-device algorithm to call emergency services after a 10-second countdown. The OECD AI Incidents Monitor lists the case as a protective response. The link to transport safety is indirect. The device alerted responders to an aviation crash it did not prevent.

details.label: Purpose
details.value: Sheng Siong rolled out its AI-driven facial recognition CCTV system in April 2024 as a measure against shoplifters. It worked with the Singapore Police Force under its Shop Theft for Retailers (STAR) program. In August 2025 it announced an extension to all 83 outlets. Staff upload the photograph of a suspect identified from footage. The system alerts store managers' phones when that person enters any branch. Sheng Siong said thefts per store rose from 4.91 in 2023 to 8 in 2024. Its CEO attributed the rise to catching cases the human eye had missed. Identifying a repeat shoplifter and flagging her return was exactly its designed purpose.

details.label: AI contribution
details.value: The system's documented contribution came after a human detection. On 10 September 2025 a staff member found discrepancies in a stock check. Colleagues reviewed CCTV and saw Tan leaving without paying. They uploaded her face. The Straits Times reports that the system “then automatically identified the other instances” of theft. That turned one observed theft into an amalgamated charge covering seven visits. On 11 September the system's alert reached the retail manager's phone when she entered. He intercepted her at the self-checkout kiosk with three unscanned bottles. The interception, the bag check, the police call, the prosecution and the restitution were human and institutional. No source names the vendor or the model, gives an accuracy figure, or reports a false match in this case.

record.summary: Sheng Siong's facial recognition matched a wine thief to six prior thefts and flagged her return; arrest, restitution, eight days' jail.
record.account: Catherine Tan Li Eng, 51, took 19 Jacob's Creek wine bottles worth about S$556 from the Sheng Siong supermarket at Block 622D Punggol Central, Singapore. She bagged them unscanned at self-checkout from 2 to 11 September 2025. On 10 September staff found stock discrepancies, reviewed closed-circuit television (CCTV) and uploaded her face to the chain's AI-driven facial recognition system. It automatically identified the earlier thefts. When she returned at noon on 11 September the retail manager got a phone alert. He stopped her at the self-checkout kiosk and found three unscanned bottles. Police arrested her. On 12 May 2026 District Judge Brenda Chua jailed her for eight days on an amalgamated theft charge after full restitution of about S$470.

produced_by: A chain-wide facial recognition layer on existing CCTV (rolled out from April 2024, extended to all 83 outlets after August 2025). Staff upload a suspect's face, and managers get app alerts when that person re-enters any branch.
A human trigger: a stock check on 10 September 2025 that revealed missing bottles. Staff then reviewed the footage and uploaded the face the same day.
A repeat offender who came back to the same outlet at noon the next day, which gave the alert something to fire on.

A manager on the premises with his phone, able to intercept at the self-checkout kiosk. A police and court process (the STAR program, an amalgamated theft charge) that turned the identification into restitution and a sentence.
must_hold: The system identifies, it does not detect. Stock counts or staff still have to notice the first theft. Sheng Siong's CEO implied as much when he said the human eye had missed cases.
Someone must act on the alert within minutes. The gain here was an interception before she left the store, not the alert itself.
The match must be right and lawful. A wrong face flagged at the door would produce a wrongful stop. No source reports a false match in this case. None names the vendor or any accuracy figure.

revisions.change: Record drafted from the OECD Monitor entry and the cited sources. the date observed is 11 September 2025, the day the system's alert led to the interception and arrest; the Monitor's 12 May 2026 is the sentencing and reporting date. Filed as benefit created or restored (identification, arrest and restitution for an identifiable organization); the 11 September interception with three unscanned bottles could be read as a small specific harm prevented, but the record's benefit is the identification of the series and the recovery of the loss. Values differ slightly by outlet: CNA about S$556, The Straits Times over $550, AsiaOne over $555; restitution is “about S$470” in CNA and “full restitution” in all three, consistent with the three bottles recovered on 11 September. No source names the vendor of the facial recognition system or a model, so developer and the model version are null; the system's design and the STAR program come from Mothership's 26 August 2025 report of CNA's rollout story, as CNA's own rollout article returned 404 at the URL found and the Yahoo syndication 404 as well. CNA and The Straits Times refused direct fetches and were read through the r.jina.ai text proxy; The Straits Times headline now reads “...caught by Sheng Siong's facial recognition system” while its URL slug and the Monitor's title read “...from Sheng Shiong caught using facial recognition system”. Malay Mail's 12 May 2026 syndication of David Sun's Straits Times piece was read once and returned 403 on re-fetch, so it is not cited; STOMP and The Independent Singapore returned 403. AsiaOne credits The Straits Times and CNA. No source discusses the PDPA or privacy aspects of the system; the record notes that the first detection was human. The October 2026 echo was found through Bing after WebSearch was exhausted and Brave and DuckDuckGo rate-limited or challenged.

data.retained_case_account: Catherine Tan Li Eng, 51, took 19 Jacob's Creek wine bottles worth about S$556 from the Sheng Siong supermarket at Block 622D Punggol Central, Singapore. She bagged them unscanned at self-checkout from 2 to 11 September 2025. On 10 September staff found stock discrepancies, reviewed closed-circuit television (CCTV) and uploaded her face to the chain's AI-driven facial recognition system. It automatically identified the earlier thefts. When she returned at noon on 11 September the retail manager got a phone alert. He stopped her at the self-checkout kiosk and found three unscanned bottles. Police arrested her. On 12 May 2026 District Judge Brenda Chua jailed her for eight days on an amalgamated theft charge after full restitution of about S$470.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: The system's documented contribution came after a human detection. On 10 September 2025 a staff member found discrepancies in a stock check. Colleagues reviewed CCTV and saw Tan leaving without paying. They uploaded her face. The Straits Times reports that the system “then automatically identified the other instances” of theft. That turned one observed theft into an amalgamated charge covering seven visits. On 11 September the system's alert reached the retail manager's phone when she entered. He intercepted her at the self-checkout kiosk with three unscanned bottles. The interception, the bag check, the police call, the prosecution and the restitution were human and institutional. No source names the vendor or the model, gives an accuracy figure, or reports a false match in this case.

fields.account: Catherine Tan Li Eng, 51, took 19 Jacob's Creek wine bottles worth about S$556 from the Sheng Siong supermarket at Block 622D Punggol Central, Singapore. She bagged them unscanned at self-checkout from 2 to 11 September 2025. On 10 September staff found stock discrepancies, reviewed closed-circuit television (CCTV) and uploaded her face to the chain's AI-driven facial recognition system. It automatically identified the earlier thefts. When she returned at noon on 11 September the retail manager got a phone alert. He stopped her at the self-checkout kiosk and found three unscanned bottles. Police arrested her. On 12 May 2026 District Judge Brenda Chua jailed her for eight days on an amalgamated theft charge after full restitution of about S$470.

fields.purpose: Sheng Siong rolled out its AI-driven facial recognition CCTV system in April 2024 as a measure against shoplifters. It worked with the Singapore Police Force under its Shop Theft for Retailers (STAR) program. In August 2025 it announced an extension to all 83 outlets. Staff upload the photograph of a suspect identified from footage. The system alerts store managers' phones when that person enters any branch. Sheng Siong said thefts per store rose from 4.91 in 2023 to 8 in 2024. Its CEO attributed the rise to catching cases the human eye had missed. Identifying a repeat shoplifter and flagging her return was exactly its designed purpose.

A manager on the premises with his phone, able to intercept at the self-checkout kiosk. A police and court process (the STAR program, an amalgamated theft charge) that turned the identification into restitution and a sentence.
must_hold: The system identifies, it does not detect. Stock counts or staff still have to notice the first theft. Sheng Siong's CEO implied as much when he said the human eye had missed cases.
Someone must act on the alert within minutes. The gain here was an interception before she left the store, not the alert itself.
The match must be right and lawful. A wrong face flagged at the door would produce a wrongful stop. No source reports a false match in this case. None names the vendor or any accuracy figure.

Technical support came from the Railway Technical Research Institute of the Japanese railways. A network of latest-generation sensors detects the earliest seismic waves. Within seconds it automatically activates safety protocols to slow or stop trains. euronews (15 Jul 2025) added that the system comprises about 20 seismic stations along 200 km, on the surface and in deep boreholes. fields.account: ANSA reported on 14 Jul 2025 that Ferrovie dello Stato's infrastructure company Rete Ferroviaria Italiana had activated Italy's first seismic early-warning system. It is on the Rome-Naples high-speed line. It was developed with the Physics Department of the University of Naples Federico II. Technical support came from the Railway Technical Research Institute of the Japanese railways. A network of latest-generation sensors detects the earliest seismic waves. Within seconds it automatically activates safety protocols to slow or stop trains. euronews (15 Jul 2025) added that the system comprises about 20 seismic stations along 200 km, on the surface and in deep boreholes. They are linked by an SDH fiber network. An advanced software intelligence instantly analyzes the data and assesses the quake's danger, per euronews. The system had been operational since 3 May 2025. In the following weeks it was tested by a magnitude 4.4 earthquake. During it, trains on the Rome-Naples line were stopped preventively. Neither article gives the date of that earthquake. ANSA does not mention artificial intelligence. The OECD AI Incidents Monitor lists the system as AI-powered and a protective response.
