fields.account: The Department of Telecommunications (DoT), Government of India, states that it designed and implemented ASTR. ASTR, the “AI and facial recognition powered Solution for Telecom SIM Subscriber Verification”, is to identify and weed out fake, forged and non-bonafide mobile connections. A PIB Chennai release of 8 May 2023 reported that ASTR identified more than 50,000 non-bonafide connections in Tamil Nadu. All were disconnected by operators, with point-of-sale details handed to the Tamil Nadu Police Cyber Crime Wing. The Hindu (PTI, 28 May 2023) quoted a senior DoT official in Patna. The official said that ASTR analysis found at least 21,800 connections exceeding the nine-per-subscriber limit in Bihar and Jharkhand. Around 17,000 of them were disconnected, and operators blacklisted 2,900 points of sale. Minister of State Dr Pemmasani Chandra Sekhar gave a Rajya Sabha written reply, posted by PIB on 7 August 2025. He said that DoT disconnected more than 82 lakh connections through ASTR after they failed re-verification. The OECD AI Incidents Monitor records the Bihar and Jharkhand deactivations as an AI Incident citing privacy, misidentification and data-protection concerns. The cumulative figure carries the reply's posting date. No independent accuracy evaluation was found.

record.title: Sky Sentinel, an AI-controlled machine-gun turret built by Ukrainian engineers, is reported to have downed four Shahed drones with one prototype; UNITED24 raises $1.5 million for 10 units
record.summary: Ukraine's Sky Sentinel, an AI-controlled heavy-machine-gun turret, is reported to have downed four Russian Shahed drones with one prototype; dates and places are withheld (May-June 2025).
record.account: Sky Sentinel is an autonomous turret, a heavy machine gun on a 360-degree mount. Its software, written by Ukrainian engineers, takes radar input and separates drones from birds. It tracks the target, computes the ballistic solution and fires without a human. UNITED24 Media, the outlet of the UNITED24 fundraising platform, reported on 26 May 2025 that one prototype had downed four Shahed drones at the front. Dates and places were withheld for security. Its $1.5 million campaign for 10 turrets at about $150,000 each was complete. Forbes (David Hambling, 27 May 2025), as relayed by Euromaidan Press on 28 May 2025, repeats the four kills. It gives a pointing precision of 17 micro-radians. The Defense Post (3 June 2025) adds that 10 to 30 units would be needed to protect a city. It adds that production is scaling to dozens a month. The Monitor's statement that a human authorizes each shot is not in any read report.

data.retained_case_account: Sky Sentinel is an autonomous turret, a heavy machine gun on a 360-degree mount. Its software, written by Ukrainian engineers, takes radar input and separates drones from birds. It tracks the target, computes the ballistic solution and fires without a human. UNITED24 Media, the outlet of the UNITED24 fundraising platform, reported on 26 May 2025 that one prototype had downed four Shahed drones at the front. Dates and places were withheld for security. Its $1.5 million campaign for 10 turrets at about $150,000 each was complete. Forbes (David Hambling, 27 May 2025), as relayed by Euromaidan Press on 28 May 2025, repeats the four kills. It gives a pointing precision of 17 micro-radians. The Defense Post (3 June 2025) adds that 10 to 30 units would be needed to protect a city. It adds that production is scaling to dozens a month. The Monitor's statement that a human authorizes each shot is not in any read report.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: Per UNITED24 Media and Forbes via Euromaidan Press, the AI does the whole engagement. It takes radar data, distinguishes drones from birds and tracks the flight path. It computes the shot with wind and target speed, and fires conventional rounds. The four kills are the makers' claim relayed by the fundraiser. No independent confirmation, footage date or location is given. The Monitor's human-authorization step does not appear in the read reports.

fields.summary: Ukraine's Sky Sentinel, an AI-controlled heavy-machine-gun turret, is reported to have downed four Russian Shahed drones with one prototype; dates and places are withheld (May-June 2025).
fields.account: Sky Sentinel is an autonomous turret, a heavy machine gun on a 360-degree mount. Its software, written by Ukrainian engineers, takes radar input and separates drones from birds. It tracks the target, computes the ballistic solution and fires without a human. UNITED24 Media, the outlet of the UNITED24 fundraising platform, reported on 26 May 2025 that one prototype had downed four Shahed drones at the front. Dates and places were withheld for security. Its $1.5 million campaign for 10 turrets at about $150,000 each was complete. Forbes (David Hambling, 27 May 2025), as relayed by Euromaidan Press on 28 May 2025, repeats the four kills. It gives a pointing precision of 17 micro-radians. The Defense Post (3 June 2025) adds that 10 to 30 units would be needed to protect a city. It adds that production is scaling to dozens a month. The Monitor's statement that a human authorizes each shot is not in any read report.

record.title: Rafael's X-Guard towed decoy, labeled “AI-powered”, may have diverted Pakistani missiles from IAF Rafales in Operation Sindoor (7–10 May 2025)
record.summary: Every account traces to ex-USAF pilot Ryan Bodenheimer via idrw.org (6 July 2025). No IAF, MoD, Dassault or Rafael confirmation; CDS Gen Anil Chauhan admitted on 31 May 2025 that India lost jets.
record.account: The OECD AI Incidents entry concerns Operation Sindoor in May 2025. It says the Indian Air Force (IAF) used “the AI-powered X-Guard decoy system on Rafale jets”. It says this “prevented enemy missiles from hitting real aircraft”. The claim originates in an idrw.org post of 6 July 2025, sourced to “AFI”, an outsourced content partner. The post quotes Ryan Bodenheimer, a former US Air Force F-15E and F-16 pilot. He calls the IAF's tactics “the best spoofing and deception we've ever seen” and credits “the Rafale's X-Guard AI-enhanced jamming decoy system”. idrw itself writes that the system “likely played a pivotal role”. It writes that Pakistani claims of downed Rafales were “likely X-Guard decoys” according to Jane's Defence Weekly. The Economic Times (ET) writes on 8 July 2025 that the IAF “reportedly used artificial intelligence-powered technology”. LatestLY (9 Jul) says it “allegedly used” it. India TV (9 Jul) attributes a finding that Pakistani kills were hits on towed decoys to “a recent Jane's Defence Weekly investigation”. No other outlet on record corroborates it, and the Jane's Defence Weekly investigation itself is not among the sources. Oneindia (9 Jul) says false claims of downed Rafales “may have been decoys”. TFIPOST (9 Jul) says the IAF “reportedly deployed” the system and names the maker correctly as Rafael Advanced Defense Systems. ET, India TV, LatestLY, Oneindia and idrw write “Rafale Advanced Defense Systems”. The Week and Business Today are quoted from an earlier reading; their pages were not available afterward. The Week's headline says the IAF “may have used” X-Guard. It describes Bodenheimer as “a military tech digital creator”. Business Today writes “reportedly misdirected”. No IAF, Ministry of Defence (MoD), Dassault or Rafael statement confirms that X-Guard was carried or deployed. Rafael's product page was not available. The claimed outcome (no losses) is contradicted by India's Chief of Defence Staff (CDS), General Anil Chauhan. At the Shangri-La Dialogue on 31 May 2025 he admitted that an unspecified number of Indian jets were shot down. He rejected Pakistan's claim of six (Al Jazeera, 1 June 2025; Wikipedia citing Bloomberg). Operation Sindoor began on 7 May 2025 and lasted four days (India TV). The Monitor's 7 July date is the coverage date.

data.retained_case_account: The OECD AI Incidents entry concerns Operation Sindoor in May 2025. It says the Indian Air Force (IAF) used “the AI-powered X-Guard decoy system on Rafale jets”. It says this “prevented enemy missiles from hitting real aircraft”. The claim originates in an idrw.org post of 6 July 2025, sourced to “AFI”, an outsourced content partner. The post quotes Ryan Bodenheimer, a former US Air Force F-15E and F-16 pilot. He calls the IAF's tactics “the best spoofing and deception we've ever seen” and credits “the Rafale's X-Guard AI-enhanced jamming decoy system”. idrw itself writes that the system “likely played a pivotal role”. It writes that Pakistani claims of downed Rafales were “likely X-Guard decoys” according to Jane's Defence Weekly. The Economic Times (ET) writes on 8 July 2025 that the IAF “reportedly used artificial intelligence-powered technology”. LatestLY (9 Jul) says it “allegedly used” it. India TV (9 Jul) attributes a finding that Pakistani kills were hits on towed decoys to “a recent Jane's Defence Weekly investigation”. No other outlet on record corroborates it, and the Jane's Defence Weekly investigation itself is not among the sources. Oneindia (9 Jul) says false claims of downed Rafales “may have been decoys”. TFIPOST (9 Jul) says the IAF “reportedly deployed” the system and names the maker correctly as Rafael Advanced Defense Systems. ET, India TV, LatestLY, Oneindia and idrw write “Rafale Advanced Defense Systems”. The Week and Business Today are quoted from an earlier reading; their pages were not available afterward. The Week's headline says the IAF “may have used” X-Guard. It describes Bodenheimer as “a military tech digital creator”. Business Today writes “reportedly misdirected”. No IAF, Ministry of Defence (MoD), Dassault or Rafael statement confirms that X-Guard was carried or deployed. Rafael's product page was not available. The claimed outcome (no losses) is contradicted by India's Chief of Defence Staff (CDS), General Anil Chauhan. At the Shangri-La Dialogue on 31 May 2025 he admitted that an unspecified number of Indian jets were shot down. He rejected Pakistan's claim of six (Al Jazeera, 1 June 2025; Wikipedia citing Bloomberg). Operation Sindoor began on 7 May 2025 and lasted four days (India TV). The Monitor's 7 July date is the coverage date.

Neither the system's AI character nor any contribution to the engagements can therefore be assessed.

fields.account: The OECD AI Incidents entry concerns Operation Sindoor in May 2025. It says the Indian Air Force (IAF) used “the AI-powered X-Guard decoy system on Rafale jets”. It says this “prevented enemy missiles from hitting real aircraft”. The claim originates in an idrw.org post of 6 July 2025, sourced to “AFI”, an outsourced content partner. The post quotes Ryan Bodenheimer, a former US Air Force F-15E and F-16 pilot. He calls the IAF's tactics “the best spoofing and deception we've ever seen” and credits “the Rafale's X-Guard AI-enhanced jamming decoy system”. idrw itself writes that the system “likely played a pivotal role”. It writes that Pakistani claims of downed Rafales were “likely X-Guard decoys” according to Jane's Defence Weekly. The Economic Times (ET) writes on 8 July 2025 that the IAF “reportedly used artificial intelligence-powered technology”. LatestLY (9 Jul) says it “allegedly used” it. India TV (9 Jul) attributes a finding that Pakistani kills were hits on towed decoys to “a recent Jane's Defence Weekly investigation”. No other outlet on record corroborates it, and the Jane's Defence Weekly investigation itself is not among the sources. Oneindia (9 Jul) says false claims of downed Rafales “may have been decoys”. TFIPOST (9 Jul) says the IAF “reportedly deployed” the system and names the maker correctly as Rafael Advanced Defense Systems. ET, India TV, LatestLY, Oneindia and idrw write “Rafale Advanced Defense Systems”. The Week and Business Today are quoted from an earlier reading; their pages were not available afterward. The Week's headline says the IAF “may have used” X-Guard. It describes Bodenheimer as “a military tech digital creator”. Business Today writes “reportedly misdirected”. No IAF, Ministry of Defence (MoD), Dassault or Rafael statement confirms that X-Guard was carried or deployed. Rafael's product page was not available. The claimed outcome (no losses) is contradicted by India's Chief of Defence Staff (CDS), General Anil Chauhan. At the Shangri-La Dialogue on 31 May 2025 he admitted that an unspecified number of Indian jets were shot down. He rejected Pakistan's claim of six (Al Jazeera, 1 June 2025; Wikipedia citing Bloomberg). Operation Sindoor began on 7 May 2025 and lasted four days (India TV). The Monitor's 7 July date is the coverage date.

record.summary: KWS installed AI-enabled FLIR thermal cameras at three black rhino sites by Sept 2024 (US State Department and WWF funding); intrusion alerts only; no AI-linked arrest or prevented event documented.
record.account: Citizen Digital reported on 21 September 2024 that the Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) had installed FLIR thermal cameras at three black rhino sites. The US Department of State Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs and WWF supported it. They are Solio Game Reserve, Lake Nakuru National Park and Ol Pejeta Conservancy, with Solio the latest and Meru National Park named next. Geoffrey Chege (WWF-Kenya) said the cameras “have inbuilt analytics that send out automated alerts every time they detect an intrusion from humans, vehicles or wildlife”. Colby Loucks of WWF-US said the cameras “can tell you when a human is in the picture or an animal” and alert rangers. KWS Director General Dr Erustus Kanga said: “I am aware that over the last six years, we have not lost a single black rhino in this sanctuary”. That predates the Solio installation. The article reports no arrest, interception or prevented poaching event attributable to the cameras.

fields.account: Citizen Digital reported on 21 September 2024 that the Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) had installed FLIR thermal cameras at three black rhino sites. The US Department of State Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs and WWF supported it. They are Solio Game Reserve, Lake Nakuru National Park and Ol Pejeta Conservancy, with Solio the latest and Meru National Park named next. Geoffrey Chege (WWF-Kenya) said the cameras “have inbuilt analytics that send out automated alerts every time they detect an intrusion from humans, vehicles or wildlife”. Colby Loucks of WWF-US said the cameras “can tell you when a human is in the picture or an animal” and alert rangers. KWS Director General Dr Erustus Kanga said: “I am aware that over the last six years, we have not lost a single black rhino in this sanctuary”. That predates the Solio installation. The article reports no arrest, interception or prevented poaching event attributable to the cameras.

fields.account: Citizen Digital reported on 21 September 2024 that the Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) had installed FLIR thermal cameras at three black rhino sites. The US Department of State Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs and WWF supported it. They are Solio Game Reserve, Lake Nakuru National Park and Ol Pejeta Conservancy, with Solio the latest and Meru National Park named next. Geoffrey Chege (WWF-Kenya) said the cameras “have inbuilt analytics that send out automated alerts every time they detect an intrusion from humans, vehicles or wildlife”. Colby Loucks of WWF-US said the cameras “can tell you when a human is in the picture or an animal” and alert rangers. KWS Director General Dr Erustus Kanga said: “I am aware that over the last six years, we have not lost a single black rhino in this sanctuary”. That predates the Solio installation. The article reports no arrest, interception or prevented poaching event attributable to the cameras.

record.title: HALO Trust pilots AWS-supported AI to find explosive remnants in drone imagery of Ukrainian minefields; it may be about 70% accurate, with no clearance outcome yet
record.summary: HALO announced a US$4m AWS package (25 June 2024) to trial AI on drone imagery of Ukrainian minefields; Reuters (30 April 2026) reports about 70% accuracy; no cleared land or found mine attributed.
record.account: The HALO Trust announced a US$4 million package of support from Amazon Web Services on 25 June 2024. An archived copy of the page, dated 20 May 2026, is among the sources. It “will enable HALO to trial artificial intelligence (AI) to assist in the process of detecting debris of war (including landmines and other explosives) in drone imagery for existing minefields and battlefields in Ukraine”. It also covers machine-learning detection of damaged buildings in satellite imagery with SageMaker. By then HALO had flown 542 drone flights over Ukrainian minefields, producing 11 terabytes of imagery. It said training would require manually labeling thousands of images and ongoing vetting by HALO staff to remove false positives and negatives. A HALO page of 21 February 2025 describes the pilot through its head of research and development, Matthew Abercrombie. He says an analyst “can take three to five days to look through the imagery for an average minefield”. It reports no results. Reuters (Sergiy Karazy, 30 April 2026, syndicated by KELO) reported from Myrotske, 40 km north-west of Kyiv. HALO “has turned to AI to analyze high-resolution drone imagery of contaminated areas and train systems to identify mines and explosive remnants, achieving around 70% accuracy already”. It quoted HALO media manager Olena Shustova. The article does not mention AWS and attributes no cleared land, found mine or time saving to the model. No later milestone is dated.

fields.account: The HALO Trust announced a US$4 million package of support from Amazon Web Services on 25 June 2024. An archived copy of the page, dated 20 May 2026, is among the sources. It “will enable HALO to trial artificial intelligence (AI) to assist in the process of detecting debris of war (including landmines and other explosives) in drone imagery for existing minefields and battlefields in Ukraine”. It also covers machine-learning detection of damaged buildings in satellite imagery with SageMaker. By then HALO had flown 542 drone flights over Ukrainian minefields, producing 11 terabytes of imagery. It said training would require manually labeling thousands of images and ongoing vetting by HALO staff to remove false positives and negatives. A HALO page of 21 February 2025 describes the pilot through its head of research and development, Matthew Abercrombie. He says an analyst “can take three to five days to look through the imagery for an average minefield”. It reports no results. Reuters (Sergiy Karazy, 30 April 2026, syndicated by KELO) reported from Myrotske, 40 km north-west of Kyiv. HALO “has turned to AI to analyze high-resolution drone imagery of contaminated areas and train systems to identify mines and explosive remnants, achieving around 70% accuracy already”. It quoted HALO media manager Olena Shustova. The article does not mention AWS and attributes no cleared land, found mine or time saving to the model. No later milestone is dated.

fields.account: The HALO Trust announced a US$4 million package of support from Amazon Web Services on 25 June 2024. An archived copy of the page, dated 20 May 2026, is among the sources. It “will enable HALO to trial artificial intelligence (AI) to assist in the process of detecting debris of war (including landmines and other explosives) in drone imagery for existing minefields and battlefields in Ukraine”. It also covers machine-learning detection of damaged buildings in satellite imagery with SageMaker. By then HALO had flown 542 drone flights over Ukrainian minefields, producing 11 terabytes of imagery. It said training would require manually labeling thousands of images and ongoing vetting by HALO staff to remove false positives and negatives. A HALO page of 21 February 2025 describes the pilot through its head of research and development, Matthew Abercrombie. He says an analyst “can take three to five days to look through the imagery for an average minefield”. It reports no results. Reuters (Sergiy Karazy, 30 April 2026, syndicated by KELO) reported from Myrotske, 40 km north-west of Kyiv. HALO “has turned to AI to analyze high-resolution drone imagery of contaminated areas and train systems to identify mines and explosive remnants, achieving around 70% accuracy already”. It quoted HALO media manager Olena Shustova. The article does not mention AWS and attributes no cleared land, found mine or time saving to the model. No later milestone is dated.

details.label: Purpose
details.value: Meta's pipeline is built to find posts indicating suicide or self-injury risk and route them to trained reviewers. In imminent cases it contacts local authorities (Meta Newsroom). The Kota arrangement routes those flags to police to intervene. This case is that purpose.

details.label: AI contribution
details.value: PTI's report says the chain starts with a red-flag tag on Meta's system when a student posts suicide or self-harm content. Account information is then shared with police. It does not say whether Meta's classifier or a user report raised the flag in the Jhunjhunu case, nor what happened on arrival. Meta's own description (2018, updated 2021) says machine-learning detection is followed by human review before authorities are contacted. The intervention itself was police work. PTI also notes that no red-flag tags had been reported in Kota city since the launch.

record.title: Kota police tie up with Meta to route suicide and self-harm flags from Facebook and Instagram to Abhay Command Centre; within a week police report a possible suicide by a Jhunjhunu student prevented
record.summary: Kota City SP Amrita Duhan said Meta's red-flag tags for suicidal posts go to a round-the-clock police team; within a week, police prevented a possible suicide by a student from Jhunjhunu (PTI).
record.account: PTI reported from Kota on 28 May 2024 that city police under Superintendent Amrita Duhan had tied up with Meta. It aims to identify students exhibiting suicidal tendencies on Facebook and Instagram. When a student posts suicide or self-harm content, a red-flag tag appears on Meta's system and account information is shared with Kota police. For students outside Kota it goes to Abhay Command Centre or the district control room. There a dedicated team works round the clock in eight-hour shifts. Within a week of the launch, police said they had prevented a possible suicide by a student from Jhunjhunu district. No red-flag tags had yet been reported in the city. PTI counted nine coaching-student suicides in 2024 to date and 26 in 2023. Duhan planned to extend the arrangement to Jaipur (PTI via LatestLY). Meta's newsroom describes machine-learning detection with human review before authorities are contacted (Card, 2018). The intervention date is not given.

data.retained_case_account: PTI reported from Kota on 28 May 2024 that city police under Superintendent Amrita Duhan had tied up with Meta. It aims to identify students exhibiting suicidal tendencies on Facebook and Instagram. When a student posts suicide or self-harm content, a red-flag tag appears on Meta's system and account information is shared with Kota police. For students outside Kota it goes to Abhay Command Centre or the district control room. There a dedicated team works round the clock in eight-hour shifts. Within a week of the launch, police said they had prevented a possible suicide by a student from Jhunjhunu district. No red-flag tags had yet been reported in the city. PTI counted nine coaching-student suicides in 2024 to date and 26 in 2023. Duhan planned to extend the arrangement to Jaipur (PTI via LatestLY). Meta's newsroom describes machine-learning detection with human review before authorities are contacted (Card, 2018). The intervention date is not given.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: PTI's report says the chain starts with a red-flag tag on Meta's system when a student posts suicide or self-harm content. Account information is then shared with police. It does not say whether Meta's classifier or a user report raised the flag in the Jhunjhunu case, nor what happened on arrival. Meta's own description (2018, updated 2021) says machine-learning detection is followed by human review before authorities are contacted. The intervention itself was police work. PTI also notes that no red-flag tags had been reported in Kota city since the launch.

fields.summary: Kota City SP Amrita Duhan said Meta's red-flag tags for suicidal posts go to a round-the-clock police team; within a week, police prevented a possible suicide by a student from Jhunjhunu (PTI).
fields.account: PTI reported from Kota on 28 May 2024 that city police under Superintendent Amrita Duhan had tied up with Meta. It aims to identify students exhibiting suicidal tendencies on Facebook and Instagram. When a student posts suicide or self-harm content, a red-flag tag appears on Meta's system and account information is shared with Kota police. For students outside Kota it goes to Abhay Command Centre or the district control room. There a dedicated team works round the clock in eight-hour shifts. Within a week of the launch, police said they had prevented a possible suicide by a student from Jhunjhunu district. No red-flag tags had yet been reported in the city. PTI counted nine coaching-student suicides in 2024 to date and 26 in 2023. Duhan planned to extend the arrangement to Jaipur (PTI via LatestLY). Meta's newsroom describes machine-learning detection with human review before authorities are contacted (Card, 2018). The intervention date is not given.

record.account: The BBC (Yvette Austin, 11 March 2024) reported on Sutton and East Surrey (SES) Water. It supplies 160 million liters a day to 300,000 homes and businesses in parts of Surrey, Kent and South London. It was among the first UK companies using AI across its whole network to reduce leaks. 1,000 underground sensors monitor flow and pressure. The technology predicts what levels should be. When a leak happens an alarm is raised within minutes and engineers deployed. Innovation manager Jeremy Heath said pipes are often repaired before customers notice a drop in pressure. Head of asset strategy Liam Ahearne said the smart network had reduced leakage run rate times by up to 40%. The BBC noted Ofwat's figure that about a fifth of water put into the network in England and Wales is lost to leakage. It gave SES Water's 2022/23 loss of 76 liters per property per day. It cited the Angling Trust's criticism that the company's targets were not good enough. The vendor and method are not named. No regulator report of a specific repaired burst was found.

data.retained_case_account: The BBC (Yvette Austin, 11 March 2024) reported on Sutton and East Surrey (SES) Water. It supplies 160 million liters a day to 300,000 homes and businesses in parts of Surrey, Kent and South London. It was among the first UK companies using AI across its whole network to reduce leaks. 1,000 underground sensors monitor flow and pressure. The technology predicts what levels should be. When a leak happens an alarm is raised within minutes and engineers deployed. Innovation manager Jeremy Heath said pipes are often repaired before customers notice a drop in pressure. Head of asset strategy Liam Ahearne said the smart network had reduced leakage run rate times by up to 40%. The BBC noted Ofwat's figure that about a fifth of water put into the network in England and Wales is lost to leakage. It gave SES Water's 2022/23 loss of 76 liters per property per day. It cited the Angling Trust's criticism that the company's targets were not good enough. The vendor and method are not named. No regulator report of a specific repaired burst was found.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: The BBC report, an independent source with named utility staff, describes the AI only in general terms (prediction of expected levels, alarms within minutes). The developer is unnamed. The 40% figure is the deployer's claim, so the AI's share of any leakage reduction is unverified.

fields.summary: SES Water installed 1,000 underground flow and pressure sensors with AI prediction that raises leak alarms within minutes; it told the BBC leakage run rate times fell by up to 40% (11 March 2024).
fields.account: The BBC (Yvette Austin, 11 March 2024) reported on Sutton and East Surrey (SES) Water. It supplies 160 million liters a day to 300,000 homes and businesses in parts of Surrey, Kent and South London. It was among the first UK companies using AI across its whole network to reduce leaks. 1,000 underground sensors monitor flow and pressure. The technology predicts what levels should be. When a leak happens an alarm is raised within minutes and engineers deployed. Innovation manager Jeremy Heath said pipes are often repaired before customers notice a drop in pressure. Head of asset strategy Liam Ahearne said the smart network had reduced leakage run rate times by up to 40%. The BBC noted Ofwat's figure that about a fifth of water put into the network in England and Wales is lost to leakage. It gave SES Water's 2022/23 loss of 76 liters per property per day. It cited the Angling Trust's criticism that the company's targets were not good enough. The vendor and method are not named. No regulator report of a specific repaired burst was found.

record.account: ScamShield is a Singapore government app by Open Government Products, a unit of GovTech. It was developed with the National Crime Prevention Council (NCPC) and the Singapore Police Force. GovInsider (June 2021) described an on-device machine-learning model that files suspected scam SMS into a junk folder. It also blocks calls from numbers on a police blocklist. It reported 722,865 SMS reported and 5,537 numbers blocked since launch, with a 95% detection accuracy claim. It quoted product manager Lennard Lim on the model's need to adapt as scammers change their attacks. Minister of State Sun Xueling gave an oral reply to parliamentary questions on 22 November 2023. She said ScamShield had about 750,000 downloads as of October 2023. About 80,000 unique scam-tainted phone numbers had been blacklisted and blocked. About 5 million SMSes had been flagged to users as potential scams. She said it has effectively protected users. She also cited about 180 million suspected scam calls blocked at network level in the first half of 2023. That is a telco measure separate from the app. No victim-level evaluation appears in the sources.

fields.account: ScamShield is a Singapore government app by Open Government Products, a unit of GovTech. It was developed with the National Crime Prevention Council (NCPC) and the Singapore Police Force. GovInsider (June 2021) described an on-device machine-learning model that files suspected scam SMS into a junk folder. It also blocks calls from numbers on a police blocklist. It reported 722,865 SMS reported and 5,537 numbers blocked since launch, with a 95% detection accuracy claim. It quoted product manager Lennard Lim on the model's need to adapt as scammers change their attacks. Minister of State Sun Xueling gave an oral reply to parliamentary questions on 22 November 2023. She said ScamShield had about 750,000 downloads as of October 2023. About 80,000 unique scam-tainted phone numbers had been blacklisted and blocked. About 5 million SMSes had been flagged to users as potential scams. She said it has effectively protected users. She also cited about 180 million suspected scam calls blocked at network level in the first half of 2023. That is a telco measure separate from the app. No victim-level evaluation appears in the sources.

fields.account: ScamShield is a Singapore government app by Open Government Products, a unit of GovTech. It was developed with the National Crime Prevention Council (NCPC) and the Singapore Police Force. GovInsider (June 2021) described an on-device machine-learning model that files suspected scam SMS into a junk folder. It also blocks calls from numbers on a police blocklist. It reported 722,865 SMS reported and 5,537 numbers blocked since launch, with a 95% detection accuracy claim. It quoted product manager Lennard Lim on the model's need to adapt as scammers change their attacks. Minister of State Sun Xueling gave an oral reply to parliamentary questions on 22 November 2023. She said ScamShield had about 750,000 downloads as of October 2023. About 80,000 unique scam-tainted phone numbers had been blacklisted and blocked. About 5 million SMSes had been flagged to users as potential scams. She said it has effectively protected users. She also cited about 180 million suspected scam calls blocked at network level in the first half of 2023. That is a telco measure separate from the app. No victim-level evaluation appears in the sources.

record.account: Response.jp reported on 11 Nov 2022 that Seibu Railway would begin full operation of a “踏切異常検知システム” on 14 Nov 2022. It combines two technologies. One is an AI monitoring system developed by OKI and Marubeni Network Solutions. It uses skeleton recognition to detect people and objects left in crossings. The other is a 3D image-analysis system from Computer Systems Laboratory that uses stereo-camera depth. When a detection occurs, the special signal lamps that warn drivers of danger operate. Live video of the site is sent to the operations control center. Operation started at three crossings on the Ikebukuro and Shinjuku lines, with two more planned within fiscal 2022. The trial that began in December 2021 was reported to have confirmed stable operation. The sources are press-release based. The OECD AI Incidents Monitor lists the deployment as an aggregate benefit. No detection event or accident outcome is documented.

fields.account: Response.jp reported on 11 Nov 2022 that Seibu Railway would begin full operation of a “踏切異常検知システム” on 14 Nov 2022. It combines two technologies. One is an AI monitoring system developed by OKI and Marubeni Network Solutions. It uses skeleton recognition to detect people and objects left in crossings. The other is a 3D image-analysis system from Computer Systems Laboratory that uses stereo-camera depth. When a detection occurs, the special signal lamps that warn drivers of danger operate. Live video of the site is sent to the operations control center. Operation started at three crossings on the Ikebukuro and Shinjuku lines, with two more planned within fiscal 2022. The trial that began in December 2021 was reported to have confirmed stable operation. The sources are press-release based. The OECD AI Incidents Monitor lists the deployment as an aggregate benefit. No detection event or accident outcome is documented.

fields.account: Response.jp reported on 11 Nov 2022 that Seibu Railway would begin full operation of a “踏切異常検知システム” on 14 Nov 2022. It combines two technologies. One is an AI monitoring system developed by OKI and Marubeni Network Solutions. It uses skeleton recognition to detect people and objects left in crossings. The other is a 3D image-analysis system from Computer Systems Laboratory that uses stereo-camera depth. When a detection occurs, the special signal lamps that warn drivers of danger operate. Live video of the site is sent to the operations control center. Operation started at three crossings on the Ikebukuro and Shinjuku lines, with two more planned within fiscal 2022. The trial that began in December 2021 was reported to have confirmed stable operation. The sources are press-release based. The OECD AI Incidents Monitor lists the deployment as an aggregate benefit. No detection event or accident outcome is documented.

record.summary: RFCx Guardian sensors detect chainsaws with AI and alert patrols; a 2021 Reuters report from Solok, West Sumatra quotes a patroller that logging stopped. No dated intervention is documented.
record.account: Rainforest Connection (RFCx), a US non-profit founded by Topher White, deploys solar-powered “Guardian” acoustic sensors. In its own words, they use “sound & artificial intelligence” to track chainsaws, vehicle engines, hunting dogs and gunshots. They send real-time alerts to a mobile app so that “an agent nearby” can respond. RFCx states it has protected over 726,000 (impact page) or 750,000 (guardian page) hectares across 8,662+ projects in 137 countries. The only non-vendor account read is a Thomson Reuters Foundation report published by The Straits Times on 11 February 2021. It is from Solok regency, West Sumatra, Indonesia, where 27 Guardian sensors had been installed more than a year earlier. Audio streams are analyzed by AI trained to pick out chainsaw sounds, and an alert goes to community patrols. Patroller Jasrialdi said logging “has totally stopped” in the area. The head of West Sumatra's forestry department, Yozarwardi Usama Putra, said he would like to expand the “early-warning system”. The same report attributes the decline in logging to a wider enforcement crackdown as well. It says RFCx planned to collect data for peer review to prove the system curbs logging. No park authority, ministry or court document records a specific alert leading to an interception, so no event is recorded.

fields.account: Rainforest Connection (RFCx), a US non-profit founded by Topher White, deploys solar-powered “Guardian” acoustic sensors. In its own words, they use “sound & artificial intelligence” to track chainsaws, vehicle engines, hunting dogs and gunshots. They send real-time alerts to a mobile app so that “an agent nearby” can respond. RFCx states it has protected over 726,000 (impact page) or 750,000 (guardian page) hectares across 8,662+ projects in 137 countries. The only non-vendor account read is a Thomson Reuters Foundation report published by The Straits Times on 11 February 2021. It is from Solok regency, West Sumatra, Indonesia, where 27 Guardian sensors had been installed more than a year earlier. Audio streams are analyzed by AI trained to pick out chainsaw sounds, and an alert goes to community patrols. Patroller Jasrialdi said logging “has totally stopped” in the area. The head of West Sumatra's forestry department, Yozarwardi Usama Putra, said he would like to expand the “early-warning system”. The same report attributes the decline in logging to a wider enforcement crackdown as well. It says RFCx planned to collect data for peer review to prove the system curbs logging. No park authority, ministry or court document records a specific alert leading to an interception, so no event is recorded.

In its own words, they use “sound & artificial intelligence” to track chainsaws, vehicle engines, hunting dogs and gunshots. They send real-time alerts to a mobile app so that “an agent nearby” can respond. RFCx states it has protected over 726,000 (impact page) or 750,000 (guardian page) hectares across 8,662+ projects in 137 countries. The only non-vendor account read is a Thomson Reuters Foundation report published by The Straits Times on 11 February 2021. It is from Solok regency, West Sumatra, Indonesia, where 27 Guardian sensors had been installed more than a year earlier. Audio streams are analyzed by AI trained to pick out chainsaw sounds, and an alert goes to community patrols. Patroller Jasrialdi said logging “has totally stopped” in the area. The head of West Sumatra's forestry department, Yozarwardi Usama Putra, said he would like to expand the “early-warning system”. The same report attributes the decline in logging to a wider enforcement crackdown as well. It says RFCx planned to collect data for peer review to prove the system curbs logging. No park authority, ministry or court document records a specific alert leading to an interception, so no event is recorded.

record.account: Mynavi News reported on 12 Aug 2020, from a press release, a field trial of AI image analysis of crossing surveillance cameras. Optage, Sanyo Electric Railway and the Sanyo Electric Railway Information Center had begun it. It ran from early August to mid-October 2020 at three crossings on Sanyo Electric Railway lines. Edge devices analyze the video in real time to detect people, including those with prams or wheelchairs. They aim to stop trains safely by signaling the driver through a special signal lamp and notifying the operations center over an IP-VPN. Accuracy in rain and at night was to be verified with K4Digital. Full deployment was targeted for spring 2021. No results are reported, and the OECD AI Incidents Monitor entry notes that no incidents had been reported.

fields.account: Mynavi News reported on 12 Aug 2020, from a press release, a field trial of AI image analysis of crossing surveillance cameras. Optage, Sanyo Electric Railway and the Sanyo Electric Railway Information Center had begun it. It ran from early August to mid-October 2020 at three crossings on Sanyo Electric Railway lines. Edge devices analyze the video in real time to detect people, including those with prams or wheelchairs. They aim to stop trains safely by signaling the driver through a special signal lamp and notifying the operations center over an IP-VPN. Accuracy in rain and at night was to be verified with K4Digital. Full deployment was targeted for spring 2021. No results are reported, and the OECD AI Incidents Monitor entry notes that no incidents had been reported.

fields.account: Mynavi News reported on 12 Aug 2020, from a press release, a field trial of AI image analysis of crossing surveillance cameras. Optage, Sanyo Electric Railway and the Sanyo Electric Railway Information Center had begun it. It ran from early August to mid-October 2020 at three crossings on Sanyo Electric Railway lines. Edge devices analyze the video in real time to detect people, including those with prams or wheelchairs. They aim to stop trains safely by signaling the driver through a special signal lamp and notifying the operations center over an IP-VPN. Accuracy in rain and at night was to be verified with K4Digital. Full deployment was targeted for spring 2021. No results are reported, and the OECD AI Incidents Monitor entry notes that no incidents had been reported.

record.account: The Maritime Executive reported on 15 Apr 2020 that Fujitsu Limited and the Japan Coast Guard had field-tested an artificial-intelligence system to predict vessel collisions. The test ran from December 2019 to March 2020 at the Tokyo Wan Vessel Traffic Service Center. It provides navigation support under an outsourcing contract with the Coast Guard. It uses Fujitsu Human Centric AI Zinrai from Fujitsu Laboratories. The technology detects near misses between vessels and predicts areas where collision risk concentrates in Tokyo Bay. In the center's training environment, six experienced maritime traffic controllers and instructors simulated control tasks based on past near-miss accidents. They compared conventional operation with operation supported by risk information computed from past AIS data and Coast Guard risk-recommendation records. It shortened the time before a controller sent a risk warning to a vessel by an average of about two minutes. The number of warnings issued to risk-prone vessels nearly doubled, and it was found particularly effective for newcomers. The article cites the Japan Transport Safety Board's count of 2,863 marine collisions in Japan from 2009 to 2019. The results come from a simulation, not live traffic.

fields.account: The Maritime Executive reported on 15 Apr 2020 that Fujitsu Limited and the Japan Coast Guard had field-tested an artificial-intelligence system to predict vessel collisions. The test ran from December 2019 to March 2020 at the Tokyo Wan Vessel Traffic Service Center. It provides navigation support under an outsourcing contract with the Coast Guard. It uses Fujitsu Human Centric AI Zinrai from Fujitsu Laboratories. The technology detects near misses between vessels and predicts areas where collision risk concentrates in Tokyo Bay. In the center's training environment, six experienced maritime traffic controllers and instructors simulated control tasks based on past near-miss accidents. They compared conventional operation with operation supported by risk information computed from past AIS data and Coast Guard risk-recommendation records. It shortened the time before a controller sent a risk warning to a vessel by an average of about two minutes. The number of warnings issued to risk-prone vessels nearly doubled, and it was found particularly effective for newcomers. The article cites the Japan Transport Safety Board's count of 2,863 marine collisions in Japan from 2009 to 2019. The results come from a simulation, not live traffic.

record.account: Odakyu Electric Railway announced on 30 March 2020 (press release republished by Nikkei) a 転落検知システム (fall detection system). It would operate from the first train on 1 April 2020 at Kyōdō (経堂) and Soshigaya-Ōkura (祖師ヶ谷大蔵) stations on the Odakyu Line. It uses video from existing station cameras. Built with Panasonic System Solutions Japan, the system applies Panasonic's image-analysis and deep-learning technology to analyze the camera feeds in real time. It alerts a dedicated terminal in the station office, showing the camera image, when it detects a person fallen from the platform onto the tracks. It does the same for a person who has stayed at the platform edge for a set time and risks contact with a train. Staff can then take safety measures such as an emergency stop. Pre-learning to set each camera's detection area and to distinguish people from trains had run at both stations since December 2019. Impress Watch reported the launch on 31 March 2020. Neither source reports any detection, prevented accident or performance figure, and no later outcome report was found. Impress Watch (7 October 2024) reported a separate trial of Asilla's behavior-recognition “AI Security asilla” on all 20 existing cameras at Kakio and Tamagawa-Gakuen-mae stations. It ran from 10 October 2024 to 9 January 2025. It tested detection of falls from the platform, wheelchair and white-cane users, people lingering on the platform, disputes between passengers and suspicious objects. Results were not reported. Romanizations of station names are ours; the sources give them in Japanese.

fields.account: Odakyu Electric Railway announced on 30 March 2020 (press release republished by Nikkei) a 転落検知システム (fall detection system). It would operate from the first train on 1 April 2020 at Kyōdō (経堂) and Soshigaya-Ōkura (祖師ヶ谷大蔵) stations on the Odakyu Line. It uses video from existing station cameras. Built with Panasonic System Solutions Japan, the system applies Panasonic's image-analysis and deep-learning technology to analyze the camera feeds in real time. It alerts a dedicated terminal in the station office, showing the camera image, when it detects a person fallen from the platform onto the tracks. It does the same for a person who has stayed at the platform edge for a set time and risks contact with a train. Staff can then take safety measures such as an emergency stop. Pre-learning to set each camera's detection area and to distinguish people from trains had run at both stations since December 2019. Impress Watch reported the launch on 31 March 2020. Neither source reports any detection, prevented accident or performance figure, and no later outcome report was found. Impress Watch (7 October 2024) reported a separate trial of Asilla's behavior-recognition “AI Security asilla” on all 20 existing cameras at Kakio and Tamagawa-Gakuen-mae stations. It ran from 10 October 2024 to 9 January 2025. It tested detection of falls from the platform, wheelchair and white-cane users, people lingering on the platform, disputes between passengers and suspicious objects. Results were not reported. Romanizations of station names are ours; the sources give them in Japanese.

fields.account: Odakyu Electric Railway announced on 30 March 2020 (press release republished by Nikkei) a 転落検知システム (fall detection system). It would operate from the first train on 1 April 2020 at Kyōdō (経堂) and Soshigaya-Ōkura (祖師ヶ谷大蔵) stations on the Odakyu Line. It uses video from existing station cameras. Built with Panasonic System Solutions Japan, the system applies Panasonic's image-analysis and deep-learning technology to analyze the camera feeds in real time. It alerts a dedicated terminal in the station office, showing the camera image, when it detects a person fallen from the platform onto the tracks. It does the same for a person who has stayed at the platform edge for a set time and risks contact with a train. Staff can then take safety measures such as an emergency stop. Pre-learning to set each camera's detection area and to distinguish people from trains had run at both stations since December 2019. Impress Watch reported the launch on 31 March 2020. Neither source reports any detection, prevented accident or performance figure, and no later outcome report was found. Impress Watch (7 October 2024) reported a separate trial of Asilla's behavior-recognition “AI Security asilla” on all 20 existing cameras at Kakio and Tamagawa-Gakuen-mae stations. It ran from 10 October 2024 to 9 January 2025. It tested detection of falls from the platform, wheelchair and white-cane users, people lingering on the platform, disputes between passengers and suspicious objects. Results were not reported. Romanizations of station names are ours; the sources give them in Japanese.

record.account: VeriPol, a model for detecting false robbery reports from their text, was developed by Complutense and Carlos III university researchers with police officer Miguel Camacho-Collados. It appeared in Knowledge-Based Systems (Quijano-Sánchez, Liberatore, Camacho-Collados and Camacho-Collados, 2018). The abstract reports a validation accuracy of 91% on more than 1,000 reports from 2015, an improvement of more than 15% over expert officers. It reports a pilot study in June 2017 showing a lower bound on empirical precision of about 83%. Scientific American (1 February 2019) reported that the one-week pilot in Murcia and Málaga detected 25 and 39 false robberies respectively. The same month over the previous decade had 3 and 12. It quoted Camacho Collados on colleagues wasting time on cases that never occurred. Civio (25 March 2025) reported that the police said that in 83.54% of reports flagged false the complainant confessed. It also reported the Interior Ministry's 2018 announcement of nationwide use. Complaints analyzed were 49,702 in 2019 with 2,338 deemed false, and 3,762 in 2022 with 511 deemed false. Use stopped on 21 October 2024 because the tool was not valid in judicial proceedings, it said. A University of Valencia report (September 2024) criticized the 1,122-report training sample, missing officer training and regional language variation. AlgorithmWatch (27 October 2020) found no independent verification of effectiveness since deployment. The pilot month carries no day.

fields.account: VeriPol, a model for detecting false robbery reports from their text, was developed by Complutense and Carlos III university researchers with police officer Miguel Camacho-Collados. It appeared in Knowledge-Based Systems (Quijano-Sánchez, Liberatore, Camacho-Collados and Camacho-Collados, 2018). The abstract reports a validation accuracy of 91% on more than 1,000 reports from 2015, an improvement of more than 15% over expert officers. It reports a pilot study in June 2017 showing a lower bound on empirical precision of about 83%. Scientific American (1 February 2019) reported that the one-week pilot in Murcia and Málaga detected 25 and 39 false robberies respectively. The same month over the previous decade had 3 and 12. It quoted Camacho Collados on colleagues wasting time on cases that never occurred. Civio (25 March 2025) reported that the police said that in 83.54% of reports flagged false the complainant confessed. It also reported the Interior Ministry's 2018 announcement of nationwide use. Complaints analyzed were 49,702 in 2019 with 2,338 deemed false, and 3,762 in 2022 with 511 deemed false. Use stopped on 21 October 2024 because the tool was not valid in judicial proceedings, it said. A University of Valencia report (September 2024) criticized the 1,122-report training sample, missing officer training and regional language variation. AlgorithmWatch (27 October 2020) found no independent verification of effectiveness since deployment. The pilot month carries no day.

fields.summary: The Spanish National Police's text-based false-report classifier flagged 25 false robberies in Murcia and 39 in Málaga in a week in June 2017 (versus 3 and 12 in the same month over the prior decad...
fields.account: VeriPol, a model for detecting false robbery reports from their text, was developed by Complutense and Carlos III university researchers with police officer Miguel Camacho-Collados. It appeared in Knowledge-Based Systems (Quijano-Sánchez, Liberatore, Camacho-Collados and Camacho-Collados, 2018). The abstract reports a validation accuracy of 91% on more than 1,000 reports from 2015, an improvement of more than 15% over expert officers. It reports a pilot study in June 2017 showing a lower bound on empirical precision of about 83%. Scientific American (1 February 2019) reported that the one-week pilot in Murcia and Málaga detected 25 and 39 false robberies respectively. The same month over the previous decade had 3 and 12. It quoted Camacho Collados on colleagues wasting time on cases that never occurred. Civio (25 March 2025) reported that the police said that in 83.54% of reports flagged false the complainant confessed. It also reported the Interior Ministry's 2018 announcement of nationwide use. Complaints analyzed were 49,702 in 2019 with 2,338 deemed false, and 3,762 in 2022 with 511 deemed false. Use stopped on 21 October 2024 because the tool was not valid in judicial proceedings, it said. A University of Valencia report (September 2024) criticized the 1,122-report training sample, missing officer training and regional language variation. AlgorithmWatch (27 October 2020) found no independent verification of effectiveness since deployment. The pilot month carries no day.

record.title: Face matches reported in a search for missing children
record.summary: The ministry reported 2,930 facial matches among children in care. The Delhi High Court later recorded that the software had not helped solve any missing-child case.
record.account: PTI reported on 22 April 2018 (Business Standard) on an affidavit from the Ministry of Women and Child Development to the Delhi High Court. It said that the Delhi Police, “on a trial basis, used the FRS on 45,000 children living in different children's homes”. Also, 2,930 children “could be recognized between April 6 and April 10”. The ministry's secretary Rakesh Srivastava said that the police shared the outcome on 10 April. In Sadhan Haldar v NCT of Delhi, the court had pressed the police to test-run facial recognition. The ministry had then supplied data on about seven lakh missing children from the Track Child portal. The same report says that identities “have been established and efforts are on to help them reunite with their families”. No reunification is documented in any cited source. The Wire (republished by the Pulitzer Center, 2–3 July 2025) cites the Bureau of Police Research and Development's Compendium of Equipment. It says that the police bought two facial recognition systems on 28 March 2018, manufactured by Innefu Labs and supplied by Pelorus Technologies. It quotes an Innefu blog claiming its AI Vision product “helped in identifying 3000 missing children” in its first four days. On 23 August 2018 Delhi Police counsel Rahul Mehra told the High Court: “The software is not good. There is only two percent match” (NDTV). That was in a habeas corpus matter about women missing from a placement agency. On 22 January 2019 the High Court (Hima Kohli and Manoj Kumar Ohri JJ) recorded in Sadhan Haldar what it was told. The software “has not helped in cracking any case of missing children so far”, against 5,160 children untraced out of 19,916 reported missing in 2016–2018. A Centre for Internet and Society (CIS India) report gives 10,617 matches, of which 3,202 identities were verified, and no reunification count.

data.retained_case_account: PTI reported on 22 April 2018 (Business Standard) on an affidavit from the Ministry of Women and Child Development to the Delhi High Court. It said that the Delhi Police, “on a trial basis, used the FRS on 45,000 children living in different children's homes”. Also, 2,930 children “could be recognized between April 6 and April 10”. The ministry's secretary Rakesh Srivastava said that the police shared the outcome on 10 April. In Sadhan Haldar v NCT of Delhi, the court had pressed the police to test-run facial recognition. The ministry had then supplied data on about seven lakh missing children from the Track Child portal. The same report says that identities “have been established and efforts are on to help them reunite with their families”. No reunification is documented in any cited source. The Wire (republished by the Pulitzer Center, 2–3 July 2025) cites the Bureau of Police Research and Development's Compendium of Equipment. It says that the police bought two facial recognition systems on 28 March 2018, manufactured by Innefu Labs and supplied by Pelorus Technologies. It quotes an Innefu blog claiming its AI Vision product “helped in identifying 3000 missing children” in its first four days. On 23 August 2018 Delhi Police counsel Rahul Mehra told the High Court: “The software is not good. There is only two percent match” (NDTV). That was in a habeas corpus matter about women missing from a placement agency. On 22 January 2019 the High Court (Hima Kohli and Manoj Kumar Ohri JJ) recorded in Sadhan Haldar what it was told. The software “has not helped in cracking any case of missing children so far”, against 5,160 children untraced out of 19,916 reported missing in 2016–2018. A Centre for Internet and Society (CIS India) report gives 10,617 matches, of which 3,202 identities were verified, and no reunification count.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: The software produced the 2,930 matches reported in the ministry's affidavit. The claim rests on the police's report of raw output, relayed by PTI, and on the vendor's blog. No cited source verifies a single match to a reunification. The police counsel described the match rate as two percent in August 2018. The Delhi High Court recorded in January 2019 that the software had not helped crack any case. The CIS India figures (10,617 matches, 3,202 identities verified) come from a report that is not among the sources.

fields.summary: The ministry reported 2,930 facial matches among children in care. The Delhi High Court later recorded that the software had not helped solve any missing-child case.
fields.account: PTI reported on 22 April 2018 (Business Standard) on an affidavit from the Ministry of Women and Child Development to the Delhi High Court. It said that the Delhi Police, “on a trial basis, used the FRS on 45,000 children living in different children's homes”. Also, 2,930 children “could be recognized between April 6 and April 10”. The ministry's secretary Rakesh Srivastava said that the police shared the outcome on 10 April. In Sadhan Haldar v NCT of Delhi, the court had pressed the police to test-run facial recognition. The ministry had then supplied data on about seven lakh missing children from the Track Child portal. The same report says that identities “have been established and efforts are on to help them reunite with their families”. No reunification is documented in any cited source. The Wire (republished by the Pulitzer Center, 2–3 July 2025) cites the Bureau of Police Research and Development's Compendium of Equipment. It says that the police bought two facial recognition systems on 28 March 2018, manufactured by Innefu Labs and supplied by Pelorus Technologies. It quotes an Innefu blog claiming its AI Vision product “helped in identifying 3000 missing children” in its first four days. On 23 August 2018 Delhi Police counsel Rahul Mehra told the High Court: “The software is not good. There is only two percent match” (NDTV). That was in a habeas corpus matter about women missing from a placement agency. On 22 January 2019 the High Court (Hima Kohli and Manoj Kumar Ohri JJ) recorded in Sadhan Haldar what it was told. The software “has not helped in cracking any case of missing children so far”, against 5,160 children untraced out of 19,916 reported missing in 2016–2018. A Centre for Internet and Society (CIS India) report gives 10,617 matches, of which 3,202 identities were verified, and no reunification count.

record.account: The case described was ongoing. Major Richard Hoffman of the Raleigh Police Department described Traffic Jam to CBN. It lets investigators link a potential victim to another victim and then to a suspect. Its image search returns historical images tied to the same phone number or similar image. Detective Rob Pereira described pulling a phone number from a Colorado police report into Traffic Jam to see where and when it had been used. This corroborated several victims' accounts of where the trafficker was taking them. Marinus co-founder Cara Jones described the tool as applying artificial intelligence to publicly available ad data. CBN states that Traffic Jam has helped recover hundreds of victims. Futurism (2018) repeats a similar claim from CEO Emily Kennedy with an 88 percent success rate. No individually attributable rescue is documented.

It lets investigators link a potential victim to another victim and then to a suspect. Its image search returns historical images tied to the same phone number or similar image. Detective Rob Pereira described pulling a phone number from a Colorado police report into Traffic Jam to see where and when it had been used. This corroborated several victims' accounts of where the trafficker was taking them. Marinus co-founder Cara Jones described the tool as applying artificial intelligence to publicly available ad data. CBN states that Traffic Jam has helped recover hundreds of victims. fields.summary: CBN (18 Oct 2017) shows Raleigh PD detectives using Traffic Jam, a CMU-born tool with facial recognition over escort ads, to corroborate a trafficker's movements; outcomes stated only as aggregates.
fields.account: The case described was ongoing. Major Richard Hoffman of the Raleigh Police Department described Traffic Jam to CBN. It lets investigators link a potential victim to another victim and then to a suspect. Its image search returns historical images tied to the same phone number or similar image. Detective Rob Pereira described pulling a phone number from a Colorado police report into Traffic Jam to see where and when it had been used. This corroborated several victims' accounts of where the trafficker was taking them. Marinus co-founder Cara Jones described the tool as applying artificial intelligence to publicly available ad data. CBN states that Traffic Jam has helped recover hundreds of victims. Futurism (2018) repeats a similar claim from CEO Emily Kennedy with an 88 percent success rate. No individually attributable rescue is documented.

record.title: OPTiM begins a trial of its “AI Physical Security Service” AI camera monitoring at two JR Kyushu stations, Wajiro and Futajima, from 10 October 2017
record.summary: OPTiM's release says its cloud AI monitors station camera video in real time, recognizing people, trains and the platform yellow line, and alerts administrators on anomalies; no results published.
record.account: OPTiM Corporation announced on 6 October 2017 a demonstration trial of its “AI Physical Security Service” from 10 October 2017. It would run at two Kyushu Railway Company (JR Kyushu) stations: 和白駅 (Wajiro) on the Kashii Line and 二島駅 (Futajima) on the Chikuho Main Line. The service, on “OPTiM Cloud IoT OS”, has AI monitor network-camera video in real time. When it detects an anomaly, it shows an alert and emails administrators. This is to reduce the burden on operators who watch many monitors and to raise safety in the station. The release includes an image of station camera analysis identifying people, trains and the yellow platform line. The release is the only source (on optim.co.jp and republished by @Press). JR Kyushu is not quoted, no trial end date, detection target list or result is given, and no later report of outcomes was found. Station romanizations are ours.

data.retained_case_account: OPTiM Corporation announced on 6 October 2017 a demonstration trial of its “AI Physical Security Service” from 10 October 2017. It would run at two Kyushu Railway Company (JR Kyushu) stations: 和白駅 (Wajiro) on the Kashii Line and 二島駅 (Futajima) on the Chikuho Main Line. The service, on “OPTiM Cloud IoT OS”, has AI monitor network-camera video in real time. When it detects an anomaly, it shows an alert and emails administrators. This is to reduce the burden on operators who watch many monitors and to raise safety in the station. The release includes an image of station camera analysis identifying people, trains and the yellow platform line. The release is the only source (on optim.co.jp and republished by @Press). JR Kyushu is not quoted, no trial end date, detection target list or result is given, and no later report of outcomes was found. Station romanizations are ours.

fields.account: OPTiM Corporation announced on 6 October 2017 a demonstration trial of its “AI Physical Security Service” from 10 October 2017. It would run at two Kyushu Railway Company (JR Kyushu) stations: 和白駅 (Wajiro) on the Kashii Line and 二島駅 (Futajima) on the Chikuho Main Line. The service, on “OPTiM Cloud IoT OS”, has AI monitor network-camera video in real time. When it detects an anomaly, it shows an alert and emails administrators. This is to reduce the burden on operators who watch many monitors and to raise safety in the station. The release includes an image of station camera analysis identifying people, trains and the yellow platform line. The release is the only source (on optim.co.jp and republished by @Press). JR Kyushu is not quoted, no trial end date, detection target list or result is given, and no later report of outcomes was found. Station romanizations are ours.

record.title: NCAR's DICast wind forecasts cut Xcel Energy's forecast error to 10.8%; Xcel estimates US$49 million saved
record.summary: NCAR's adaptive forecast-blending system (DICast), used by Xcel Energy since 2009, cut mean wind forecast error from about 18% to 10.8% by 2014; Xcel estimated US$49m saved (IEEE Spectrum 2015).
record.account: Sue Ellen Haupt and William Mahoney of the National Center for Atmospheric Research wrote in IEEE Spectrum (22 October 2015). NCAR's wind power forecasting system for Xcel Energy blends numerical weather models with the Dynamic Integrated foreCast (DICast) system, used for wind prediction since 2009. DICast constantly checks its predictions against outcomes and adjusts its bias corrections and weightings. The mean forecast error at a typical wind farm fell from about 18 percent in 2008 to 10.8 percent by 2014. Xcel estimated the improvements had saved customers US$49 million so far. A UCAR news item (7 February 2012) said the system saved ratepayers $6 million in 2010 alone. It described the work as building on NCAR research ranging from statistics to artificial intelligence. E&E News (4 December 2017) quoted Haupt that the forecasts could save $10 million a year. It reported that Xcel operators decommit large coal units when sustained wind is predicted. None of the sources describes the system as machine learning in so many words. The savings are Xcel's estimates reported through NCAR and the press, not a regulator's audit.

data.retained_case_account: Sue Ellen Haupt and William Mahoney of the National Center for Atmospheric Research wrote in IEEE Spectrum (22 October 2015). NCAR's wind power forecasting system for Xcel Energy blends numerical weather models with the Dynamic Integrated foreCast (DICast) system, used for wind prediction since 2009. DICast constantly checks its predictions against outcomes and adjusts its bias corrections and weightings. The mean forecast error at a typical wind farm fell from about 18 percent in 2008 to 10.8 percent by 2014. Xcel estimated the improvements had saved customers US$49 million so far. A UCAR news item (7 February 2012) said the system saved ratepayers $6 million in 2010 alone. It described the work as building on NCAR research ranging from statistics to artificial intelligence. E&E News (4 December 2017) quoted Haupt that the forecasts could save $10 million a year. It reported that Xcel operators decommit large coal units when sustained wind is predicted. None of the sources describes the system as machine learning in so many words. The savings are Xcel's estimates reported through NCAR and the press, not a regulator's audit.

fields.summary: NCAR's adaptive forecast-blending system (DICast), used by Xcel Energy since 2009, cut mean wind forecast error from about 18% to 10.8% by 2014; Xcel estimated US$49m saved (IEEE Spectrum 2015).
fields.account: Sue Ellen Haupt and William Mahoney of the National Center for Atmospheric Research wrote in IEEE Spectrum (22 October 2015). NCAR's wind power forecasting system for Xcel Energy blends numerical weather models with the Dynamic Integrated foreCast (DICast) system, used for wind prediction since 2009. DICast constantly checks its predictions against outcomes and adjusts its bias corrections and weightings. The mean forecast error at a typical wind farm fell from about 18 percent in 2008 to 10.8 percent by 2014. Xcel estimated the improvements had saved customers US$49 million so far. A UCAR news item (7 February 2012) said the system saved ratepayers $6 million in 2010 alone. It described the work as building on NCAR research ranging from statistics to artificial intelligence. E&E News (4 December 2017) quoted Haupt that the forecasts could save $10 million a year. It reported that Xcel operators decommit large coal units when sustained wind is predicted. None of the sources describes the system as machine learning in so many words. The savings are Xcel's estimates reported through NCAR and the press, not a regulator's audit.

record.title: TIAA’s AI flags a suspected scam involving a 76-year-old’s retirement savings, and staff stop the money from moving
record.summary: TIAA’s CEO said that an AI flag, staff intervention, and contact with a participant’s daughter protected retirement savings of more than $3 million.
record.account: TIAA CEO Thasunda Brown Duckett told Fortune that an AI alert helped staff stop a scam involving a 76-year-old participant’s retirement savings. A portfolio manager referred the concern to the fraud team, which spent hours with the participant and contacted his daughter. Duckett said that the money did not move. The interview describes retirement holdings above $3 million, but does not itemize an attempted transfer. The original episode was released on June 17, 2026, with its transcript published five days later. No participant statement, transaction record, or separate investigation is supplied.

record.title: NHC blended Google DeepMind's AI ensemble into official Hurricane Melissa forecasts before its Category 5 landfall in Jamaica
record.summary: NHC blended Google DeepMind's AI ensemble into official Melissa forecasts from its first advisory on 21 October 2025; Cat 5 landfall in Jamaica 28 October 2025.
record.account: The US National Hurricane Center (NHC) blended Google DeepMind's experimental AI hurricane model (ensemble mean GDMI) into official forecasts for Tropical Storm Melissa. It did so from its first advisory, 21 October 2025. Discussion 1 placed the official track between the DeepMind ensemble mean and the consensus aid HCCA. Discussion 2 described the track as a blend of the DeepMind mean, HCCA and TVCA. Discussion 8 (23 October) moved the track toward a blend of the DeepMind mean and HCCA. Discussion 10 blended the HCCA and GDMI aids. It set an intensity forecast in best agreement with GDMI after all 50 DeepMind members showed a major hurricane. On 28 October 2025 Melissa made landfall in southwestern Jamaica near New Hope with 185 mph winds and 892 mb pressure. IFRC reported 45 deaths and about 1.6 million people affected. It relayed a World Bank/IDB estimate of US$8.8 billion in physical damage. Its CHF 80,000 Imminent DREF was approved on 23 October with a five-day lead time.

data.retained_case_account: The US National Hurricane Center (NHC) blended Google DeepMind's experimental AI hurricane model (ensemble mean GDMI) into official forecasts for Tropical Storm Melissa. It did so from its first advisory, 21 October 2025. Discussion 1 placed the official track between the DeepMind ensemble mean and the consensus aid HCCA. Discussion 2 described the track as a blend of the DeepMind mean, HCCA and TVCA. Discussion 8 (23 October) moved the track toward a blend of the DeepMind mean and HCCA. Discussion 10 blended the HCCA and GDMI aids. It set an intensity forecast in best agreement with GDMI after all 50 DeepMind members showed a major hurricane. On 28 October 2025 Melissa made landfall in southwestern Jamaica near New Hope with 185 mph winds and 892 mb pressure. IFRC reported 45 deaths and about 1.6 million people affected. It relayed a World Bank/IDB estimate of US$8.8 billion in physical damage. Its CHF 80,000 Imminent DREF was approved on 23 October with a five-day lead time.

fields.account: The US National Hurricane Center (NHC) blended Google DeepMind's experimental AI hurricane model (ensemble mean GDMI) into official forecasts for Tropical Storm Melissa. It did so from its first advisory, 21 October 2025. Discussion 1 placed the official track between the DeepMind ensemble mean and the consensus aid HCCA. Discussion 2 described the track as a blend of the DeepMind mean, HCCA and TVCA. Discussion 8 (23 October) moved the track toward a blend of the DeepMind mean and HCCA. Discussion 10 blended the HCCA and GDMI aids. It set an intensity forecast in best agreement with GDMI after all 50 DeepMind members showed a major hurricane. On 28 October 2025 Melissa made landfall in southwestern Jamaica near New Hope with 185 mph winds and 892 mb pressure. IFRC reported 45 deaths and about 1.6 million people affected. It relayed a World Bank/IDB estimate of US$8.8 billion in physical damage. Its CHF 80,000 Imminent DREF was approved on 23 October with a five-day lead time.

fields.summary: NHC blended Google DeepMind's AI ensemble into official Melissa forecasts from its first advisory on 21 October 2025; Cat 5 landfall in Jamaica 28 October 2025.
fields.account: The US National Hurricane Center (NHC) blended Google DeepMind's experimental AI hurricane model (ensemble mean GDMI) into official forecasts for Tropical Storm Melissa. It did so from its first advisory, 21 October 2025. Discussion 1 placed the official track between the DeepMind ensemble mean and the consensus aid HCCA. Discussion 2 described the track as a blend of the DeepMind mean, HCCA and TVCA. Discussion 8 (23 October) moved the track toward a blend of the DeepMind mean and HCCA. Discussion 10 blended the HCCA and GDMI aids. It set an intensity forecast in best agreement with GDMI after all 50 DeepMind members showed a major hurricane. On 28 October 2025 Melissa made landfall in southwestern Jamaica near New Hope with 185 mph winds and 892 mb pressure. IFRC reported 45 deaths and about 1.6 million people affected. It relayed a World Bank/IDB estimate of US$8.8 billion in physical damage. Its CHF 80,000 Imminent DREF was approved on 23 October with a five-day lead time.

record.title: UNEP MARS alert led to repair of a decades-old methane source at Hassi Messaoud, Algeria, verified by satellite from 15 October 2024
record.summary: MARS alert led an Algerian operator to fix an unlit flare at Hassi Messaoud; satellites show no emissions since 15 October 2024.
record.account: UNEP's Methane Alert and Response System (MARS) combines data from more than 30 satellite instruments with expert analysis and AI models. It confirmed mitigation of a methane source at Hassi Messaoud, Algeria, in October 2024. UNEP's case document was issued in November 2024 per the repository record. The PDF's last-updated field reads 15 October 2024. It records a Landsat 5 detection dated 1 July 1987. It attributes the emissions to an unlit flare caused by a passing valve on the flare line. The operator corrected the valve and restored normal operations. UNEP states no further emissions have been detected at the location since 15 October 2024. UN News reported on 23 July 2026 that the Algerian alert led to the repair of a leak that had persisted for decades.

data.retained_case_account: UNEP's Methane Alert and Response System (MARS) combines data from more than 30 satellite instruments with expert analysis and AI models. It confirmed mitigation of a methane source at Hassi Messaoud, Algeria, in October 2024. UNEP's case document was issued in November 2024 per the repository record. The PDF's last-updated field reads 15 October 2024. It records a Landsat 5 detection dated 1 July 1987. It attributes the emissions to an unlit flare caused by a passing valve on the flare line. The operator corrected the valve and restored normal operations. UNEP states no further emissions have been detected at the location since 15 October 2024. UN News reported on 23 July 2026 that the Algerian alert led to the repair of a leak that had persisted for decades.

retained_ai_contribution_statement.statement: UNEP IMEO both developed and operates MARS (developer and deployer are the same body). UNEP's MARS page describes detection using more than 30 satellite instruments coupled with expertise and advanced AI models. The MARS FAQ says deep learning models monitor high-resolution satellite data for further emissions. The case document's boilerplate says MARS combines 30+ satellite instruments with expert analysis and AI models. None of these states which step in this case was AI-driven. The repair was carried out by the operator. The two case-document items are treated as a public body's official reports rather than vendor material.

IFAW and Baidu report that AI Guardian screened 360,000 images and helped remove 7,853 illegal wildlife postings by mid-2024.

Removed postings are not confirmed prevented sales or animals protected. The November 2024 version’s stated 86% accuracy across 34 species lacks a test denominator, species-level errors, and false-removal analysis. Relisting, human review, and a no-tool comparison remain unassessed.
